Buttons: **Make that change** and **Leave it as is**. Accepting changes the threshold in place. The rule keeps its name and fire count. From the next run it applies only to nights above the new number, so nights between the old and new numbers lose its change (or gain it, if the number went down).

Never tuned: a rule whose occupancy condition uses **Less than**, a rule with no occupancy condition (a booking window rule on its own, say), and any rule with a booking speed or pickup condition. A rule that pairs **Greater than** with a booking window condition can be tuned, and the card moves only its occupancy threshold, never the booking window.

**Example: The exact levels, for the curious**

MAYA takes the occupancy of every past night that had at least one booking (rooms booked over all your active room types' rooms). Nights with no bookings are left out. The first level is the point 80 in 100 of your nights stay under, held between 60 and 85. The second is the point 95 in 100 stay under, held between 10 above the first and 95. Both are rounded to the nearest 5.

Offered for a room type whose floor or ceiling is still at MAYA's default, when there is a number to offer: your answer from the five questions, or enough history (30 nights for a floor, 200 for a ceiling). Room types whose name or bookings look unlike a bedroom never get one, even after you confirm they are rooms.

The defaults are 1.00 for a floor and 99,999.99 for a ceiling, in your property's currency. Any ceiling of 99,000 or more counts as the default, so in a currency such as yen a ceiling you set yourself can still get a card. Read its number before you accept it.

The card gives the reason and a suggested amount in an editable box. Press **Set it to 80** to accept it, or type your own number and the button follows. **No thanks** keeps the default. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28) for where the numbers come from and how to set a limit when no card comes.

Answered cards are counted as "N items already handled" and are not shown again on this read. A later read may ask about typos, $0 rates or deleted room types again, and will offer the starter rules again if you still have no booking speed rule. Press **Finish** or close the page. Read [Checking what MAYA found](@26).

**Not yet** · You cannot ask for one kind of suggestion on its own, or run the read on a schedule. There are no suggestions for a booking window threshold, for occupancy rules that use **Less than**, or for a rule's percentage. And a suggestion never edits a rule's room types or dates.

**Example: Priya runs it at The Harbour Inn**

Priya, the Revenue Manager, built "Busy nights" at Greater than 60. She also built a pickup rule called "Quick pickup" that raises Standard, Deluxe and Suite (the builder's default: the types that count as rooms) by 10% when a night gains more than 4 room nights in 3 days. The five starter rules are on. She presses **Get suggestions from my data**, then the start button, and moves to the **Calendar** tab while the read runs. Later she opens **Rules** again and the button reads "2 suggestions ready →". The review shows "Tune "Busy nights"?", offering to move the trigger from 60% to 75% because that is where the inn's nights become scarce, and "Remove "Quick pickup"?", because Warm-date bump already measures and changes the same room types on every day. Had she added the Meeting Room to Quick pickup, there would be no removal card, because Warm-date bump leaves the Meeting Room out.

Open the **Rules** tab, click **+ Add a rule**, name it, pick a condition, choose raise or lower and by how much, pick the room types, and click **Add Rule**. The rule is on straight away. While your property is in simulation, MAYA shows what the rule would do without sending anything. After you go live, it sends the prices to Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations. Nothing is sent to Mews yet.

A rule is one sentence you write once: when a night looks like this, change its price by that much. About every five minutes MAYA checks every rule against your bookings, for tonight and the next 59 nights, and writes down what it did in the **Change Log** tab.

Rules live on the **Rules** tab. From the top down you will find:

- the heading **Pricing Rules**, with the **Get suggestions from my data** button beside it
- a filter with three choices, **All**, **Enabled** and **Disabled**
- a closed panel called **How rules behave**, which holds two short animations
- the list of your rules
- the **+ Add a rule** button, which opens the rule builder underneath the list

You need to be a Revenue Manager, General Manager or Hotel Admin on the property to add a rule. A Viewer can open the form, but the save is refused.

We will build a rule called "Busy nights" for The Harbour Inn, a made-up 20-room property: when a night is more than 80% full, raise every room type by 10%.

**1. Open the rule builder**

Go to the **Rules** tab and click **+ Add a rule**. The form opens underneath the list of rules.

**2. Name it**

In **Rule name**, type Busy nights. The name is how you will find the rule in the change log later, so choose words you will recognise in a month.

**3. Set the condition**

Under **Conditions**, one row is already there. Leave **Metric** on **Sellable occupancy (%)**, leave **Compare** on **Greater than**, and leave **Threshold** at 80. Read together, the row says: when more than 80% of the rooms you can sell that night are booked.

**6. Add it**

Click **Add Rule**. The rule appears in the list with its switch on **On**, and the form clears, ready for the next rule.

That is a complete rule. From the next check, about five minutes away, any night in the next 60 with sellable occupancy above 80% has its price raised by 10% for every room type you picked. When a night drops back to 80% or under, the raise comes off again.

**Careful** · A new rule is on the moment you add it. If your property is live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, its first price changes go to your system on the next cycle. Nothing is sent to Mews. If you would rather look first, build the rule in the **Rate Simulator** tab instead. A rule saved from there arrives on the Rules tab switched off. Read [Trying rules out in the Rate Simulator](@43).

The list has seven columns: **Name**, **Fired**, **Conditions**, **Room Types**, **Price Change**, **Status**, and a **Delete** button at the end of the row.

| Column | What it shows for "Busy nights" |
|---|---|
| Name | Busy nights |
| Fired | A dash until the rule has acted, then a count such as 3× |
| Conditions | Occupancy above 80% |
| Room Types | Standard, Deluxe, Suite |
| Price Change | +10% |
| Status | On |

The **Fired** count goes up once for every night and room type the rule acts on. So if "Busy nights" raises two Fridays for Standard, Deluxe and Suite, **Fired** reads 6×. A new rule whose condition already holds on many nights can show a big number within minutes: 20 nights across 3 room types is 60×. It keeps counting changes that later come off. The list is sorted with the most fired rule first, then rules that are on before rules that are off, then by name. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@41) for the rest of the list.

Open the **Change Log** tab. Each pricing run lists the prices that changed, room type by room type. When "Busy nights" acts on a Standard room at The Harbour Inn, the entry reads:

"Busy nights" raised this night 10%, from $150.00 to $165.00.
It was 85% full, past the 80% mark you set.

In simulation the same entries appear. They show what the rule would have sent. After you go live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, the same entries are what was sent.

Twelve rooms, three out of service, eight booked: 89% sellable occupancy, so a Greater than 80 rule fires.

**Example: Busy nights on three nights at The Harbour Inn**

The Harbour Inn has 20 rooms across Standard (12), Deluxe (6) and Suite (2). "Busy nights" measures all 20 together, because occupancy is worked out over the room types the rule measures.
If two Friday guests cancel, Friday drops to 15 of 20, 75%, and on the next check the raise comes off. Standard goes back to $150.

How much a rule raises or cuts is your choice. There is no right number, and MAYA does not pick one for you. The builder starts at 10%, which is $15 on The Harbour Inn's $150 Standard. Three things help you settle on yours:
- **Use the starter rules as a reference.** They cut by 7% and 15% and raise by 10% and 25%. Read [Your starter rules](@27).
Use the starter rules as a reference
- **Try it before it counts.** In the **Rate Simulator**, make up a night and see what each room type becomes. Then watch a week of the change log in simulation before you go live.
Try it before it counts

- **Remember what stacks.** Percentages compound: $200 raised 10% and then 25% is $275, not $270. A booking speed rule can fire again after each wait, so two 10% raises on $150 make $181.50. The ceiling stops raises and the floor stops cuts, so check those first. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
Remember what stacks

Each of these is a short recipe with exact labels.

1. **A last-minute cut.** When a night is close and still quiet, lower the price. **Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 3, plus **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Less than** 50, then **Decrease the rate** by 15%. Read [Price last-minute nights differently](@76).
A last-minute cut

2. **A booking speed raise.** When a night is booking faster than similar past nights did at the same point, raise it. **Booking speed (recommended)**, **Speed** **Faster Than Normal**, **Measured over** **Past week**, then **Increase the rate** by 10%. Read [Booking speed](@34) first, so the levels make sense.
A booking speed raise

3. **Suites that follow your standard rooms.** Tick **Change prices on different room types**, measure Standard, change Suite. Read [Let suites follow your standard rooms](@77).

**Not yet** · Rules run every day of the year, for every night in the window. You cannot yet limit a rule to weekends, a date range or a season, and you cannot edit a rule from the builder once it is saved. The only change made in place is accepting a "Tune ... ?" suggestion after **Get suggestions from my data**, which moves an occupancy threshold. Read [What rules cannot do yet](@44) for each limit and what to do instead.
Suites that follow your standard rooms

- [How rules run](@39): the five-minute cycle, the 60-night window, and how two rules combine on one night.
- [Simulation mode](@53): what "not sent" means, and how to go live when you are ready.

A rule has a name, one to four conditions that must all be true, a direction and an amount, and the room types it changes. The four conditions are sellable occupancy, booking speed, booking window and pickup count, one of each at most. The amount is a percent or a fixed amount, one or the other. Click **Add Rule** and the rule is on.

On the **Rules** tab, click **+ Add a rule** under the list of rules. The form opens below the button and stays open until you click the button again. Everything you type stays in the form, even if you close it or switch to another tab and back, until you click **Add Rule** or reload the page. The room type chips go back to their starting selection when you switch property, or when you change **Counts as a room** or rooms out of service on the **PMS** tab.

The **Rule name** box is required. The placeholder reads "e.g. Weekend surge". There is no length limit. The name appears in the rules list, in every change log sentence the rule writes, and in the banner MAYA shows when a rule keeps adjusting a night, so choose something you will recognise later.

The **Conditions** section is headed "Matches when all of the following are true." That sentence is the whole logic: a rule with two conditions acts only on nights where both hold. There is no either/or. If you want "busy or last-minute", make two rules.

A rule needs at least one condition and can have four at most, one of each kind. The first row is there when the form opens, set to occupancy. Click **+ Add condition** to add another row. Each new row starts on the next kind you have not used yet, in this order: occupancy, booking speed, booking window, pickup. Once a kind is used, it is greyed out in the other rows' **Metric** dropdown. When all four are in use, the button disappears.

| Metric label | What it measures | Fields on the row | Read more |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sellable occupancy (%)** | Rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell that night | **Compare** (**Greater than** or **Less than**), **Threshold**, default Greater than 80 | [Sellable occupancy](@32) |
| **Booking speed (recommended)** | How many bookings the night received recently, compared with similar past nights at the same point | **Speed** (seven levels, default **Faster Than Normal**), **Measured over** (default **Past week**), **Then waits (advanced)** (default **1 week**) | [Booking speed](@34) |
| **Booking window (days to stay)** | Days until the stay, on your property's own calendar (today is 0) | **Compare**, **Threshold**, default Greater than 7 | [Booking window](@33) |
| **Pickup count (advanced)** | Room nights (or revenue) the night gained in the last 1, 3 or 7 days | **Compare**, **Threshold** (default Greater than 5), **Lookback window** (default **3 days**), **Pickup measures** (default **Room nights (units)**) | [Pickup count (advanced)](@37) |

A few things about the number fields:

- **Threshold** must be 0 or more. If it is blank or below 0, your browser stops the save and points at the box. A typed 0 is accepted.
- Comparisons are strict. **Greater than** 80 means more than 80, not 80 exactly. **Less than** 7 means 6 or fewer.
- An occupancy threshold above 100 is saved as 100. A booking window threshold is rounded to whole days.
- Booking speed has no **Compare** field. Picking a level above Normal means "that fast or faster", a level below Normal means "that slow or slower", and **Normal** means exactly Normal.

**Good to know** · Beside **Measured over** and **Then waits (advanced)** there is a "?" you can hover or focus. It opens a short panel that says how booking speed is counted and what the wait does. The same words are on the [Booking speed](@34) page.

The **Rate adjustment** section has a dropdown and two boxes.

**Direction (required)** starts blank on purpose, showing "Choose: increase or decrease the rate…". Pick **Increase the rate** or **Decrease the rate**. If you leave it blank, your browser stops the save and points at the dropdown.

**Adjust by percent (%)** is a checkbox with a number box beside it. It starts ticked with 10. A percent change multiplies the price: 10% on $150 gives $165, and when two percent rules land on the same night they compound (10% then 25% on $200 gives $275, not $270).

**Adjust by fixed amount ($)** is a checkbox with a number box. It starts unticked. A fixed amount adds to or subtracts from the price: $25 on $150 gives $175. The box shows a $ sign whatever your property's currency. The amount is in your property's currency.

**"Is there a limit on how big a raise or cut can be?"** Not one you would meet: any amount above 0 saves in either box, up to just under 1,000,000. A raise stops at the room type's ceiling. A cut that would take the price below the floor publishes the floor instead. A cut of 100% or more, or a fixed cut as big as the price, takes the price to 0 or below on its own, so the room type's floor is published, and the floor is 1.00 in your property's currency until you set one. A typo such as 150 for 15 on a cut rule does exactly that. Set real floors before you use large cuts, and read the number again before you click **Add Rule**. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).

**Careful: An amount of 0 cannot be saved** · The form accepts 0 in either box, but MAYA refuses to store a rule that changes the price by nothing. The save fails and the error appears in red under the form. Type a real amount.

The **Apply to room types** field is a row of chips, one per active room type. A selected chip is highlighted. Above the chips a short summary reads "All room types", "K of N room types", "None selected" or, before your room types have loaded, "No room types loaded". The **Select all** and **Clear** buttons do what they say.

When the form opens, every room type that counts as a room is selected. A type you have unticked under **Counts as a room** on the **PMS** tab shows a small "not a room" tag on its chip, and hovering it reads "Meeting Room, not counted as a room (change this in the PMS tab)". It is left out of a new rule unless you click it. You can price it: a rule that changes the Meeting Room changes its price like any other type. What MAYA never does is measure it. Occupancy, booking speed and pickup are counted only over room types that count as rooms.

With one list, the rule changes every selected type and measures the selected types that count as rooms. If you select only types that do not count as rooms, the rule can still change their prices but has nothing to measure. An occupancy, booking speed or pickup condition then never holds, so the rule never fires. A rule whose only condition is booking window still fires, because it counts days, not bookings. To move the Meeting Room's price with how busy your rooms are, use the split described next: measure your rooms and change the Meeting Room.

Under the chips is a checkbox, **Change prices on different room types**. Ticking it splits the field into a **Measure** list and a **Change** list, so a rule can watch your standard rooms and price your suites. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

Click **Add Rule**. If everything is in order:

- the rule is saved and switched **On**
- it appears in the list above, in the sort order the list uses (most fired first, then on before off, then by name)
- the form clears back to its defaults and stays open, ready for the next rule

The rule runs from the next pricing check, about five minutes away, on tonight and the next 59 nights. If the property is in simulation, the change log shows what it would have sent. If the property is live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, changed prices go to your property system on the next cycle. On Mews nothing is sent, and the change log shows what the rule did.

From the next check, a night 0, 1 or 2 days away with fewer than half its sellable rooms booked is lowered by 15%: Standard $150 becomes $127.50. A night that is 2 days away but 60% full is left alone, because both conditions must hold.

**Example: Every message this form can show, and what to do**

| Message | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Your browser's own note beside a field, such as "Please fill out this field." or "Value must be greater than or equal to 0." | The name, a **Threshold** or **Direction (required)** is empty, or a threshold or amount is below 0. The wording depends on your browser | Fill in the field it points at, with a number of 0 or more |
| Enter a percentage adjustment, or turn off %. | The percent box is ticked but empty | Type a percent, or untick the box |
| Enter a dollar adjustment, or turn off $. | The fixed amount box is ticked but empty | Type an amount, or untick the box |
| Enable at least one rate adjustment (% or $). | Both boxes unticked | Tick one and type an amount |
| Select at least one room type. | No chip selected | Click a room type |

Revenue Managers, General Managers and Hotel Admins can add, switch and delete rules. A Viewer sees the same form and the same controls, but MAYA refuses a Viewer's save. The rule is not created and a permission message appears in red under the form. A Viewer who clicks a rule's switch or **Delete** sees no error, and nothing changes either. Read [Roles: who can do what](@63).

**Not yet** · Once saved, a rule cannot be edited from the builder. Delete it (which undoes the price changes it made) and add it again. The only change made in place is accepting a "Tune ... ?" suggestion after **Get suggestions from my data**, which moves an occupancy threshold. There is no date range, no weekday choice and no priority control in the builder. Read [What rules cannot do yet](@44).

Sellable occupancy is rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell that night. Only room types you have ticked as rooms count, and rooms out of service are taken off first. Twelve rooms, three out of service, eight booked: 89%. **Greater than** 80 means more than 80, not 80 exactly.

For each night, MAYA counts two things over the room types a rule measures:

- **Booked**: how many rooms are on the books for that night. A booking that holds several rooms counts each room.
Booked

- **Sellable**: how many rooms you could sell that night. That is the room type's room count, minus any rooms you have marked out of service for that night.

Sellable occupancy is booked divided by sellable, as a percentage.

**Example: Twelve Standard rooms at The Harbour Inn**

Standard has 12 rooms. Three are out of service for a repair this week. Eight are booked for Friday.

Booked 8, sellable 12 minus 3, which is 9. Eight of nine is 89% sellable occupancy. A rule set to **Greater than** 80 fires.

Without the out-of-service block, the same night is 8 of 12, which is 67%, and the rule does not fire.

The rule builder's label for this condition is **Sellable occupancy (%)**. Its fields are **Compare** (**Greater than** or **Less than**) and **Threshold**, which starts at 80.

Twelve rooms, three out of service, eight booked: 89% sellable occupancy, so a Greater than 80 rule fires.
Sellable

MAYA reads your bookings from your property system about every five minutes. Which bookings count as booked depends on the system.

**Cloudbeds:** Bookings with the status confirmed, checked in, checked out or "Confirmation Pending" (Cloudbeds calls it not confirmed) count as booked. That matches how Cloudbeds' own occupancy counts them. Cancelled bookings and no-shows do not count.

**ThinkReservations:** Every booking counts as booked except cancelled bookings and no-shows.

**Mews:** Every Mews reservation counts as booked, including enquiries and optional (tentative) and requested ones. Only cancelled reservations are left out. Read [Which bookings count](@14#which-bookings-count).

A cancelled booking disappears from the count on the next read. It is not counted as a negative.

A booking counts by its status, not its rate, so a comp, house-use or owner stay at $0 counts as a booked room like any other. A day-use booking (in and out the same day) counts as a booked room on its date too: always in ThinkReservations and Mews, and in Cloudbeds when Cloudbeds lists a room rate for that date. Read [Comp, house-use and day-use bookings](@22#comp-house-use-and-day-use-bookings).

Room blocks, allotments and rooms held without a booking are not read from any property system. If you want a held block to reduce what MAYA counts as sellable, enter those rooms as out of service.

Only room types ticked as **Counts as a room** on the **PMS** tab go into the sellable count. A meeting room, a spa slot or a court that you have unticked never adds to the rooms MAYA divides by, and its bookings never add to the booked count. It can still be priced by a rule that changes it. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@51).

When a rule measures a type that does not count as a room, MAYA leaves that type out of the occupancy figure and says so in the change log: "That 95% leaves out Meeting Room." Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

On the **PMS** tab, under each room type, **+ Rooms out of service** lets you take some rooms off sale for a stretch of nights. Those rooms come off the sellable count for those nights only, so an occupancy rule reads against what you can sell. Nothing is sent to your property system about the block. Saving or clearing a block re-prices straight away. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@51).

Sellable occupancy can read above 100%. It happens when you mark rooms out of service after they were already sold, or when your property system has overbooked a night. Twelve rooms, three out of service, ten booked: 111%.

You cannot set a threshold above 100 in the builder. A number above 100 is saved as 100. A rule set to **Greater than** 100 fires on any overbooked night.

The comparison is strict. **Greater than** 80 fires at 80.01% and does not fire at 80.00%. **Less than** 50 fires at 49.9% and does not fire at 50.00%. To include 80% itself, set the threshold to 79.99 (the box takes decimals). A threshold of 79 would also fire at 79.5%, for example 159 of 200 rooms.

Occupancy is worked out over the room types a rule measures, not over the whole property. A rule that measures only Deluxe reads Deluxe's occupancy. The day card on the **Calendar** tab shows occupancy over every room type that counts as a room. So the day card can say 85% while a rule that measures only Standard sees 75% and does not fire. When you wonder why a rule did not fire, check which room types it measures.

- **The day card** on the **Calendar** tab: "17/20 rooms · 85% sellable occupancy · revenue on the books $4,850.00". The room count there is the sellable count over the types that count as rooms. The day card always shows a $ sign, whatever your property's currency.
The day card

- **The change log**: "It was 83% full, past the 80% mark you set." or "under the 40% mark you set". With a booking window on the same rule: "It was 95% full with 17 days to go, past the 90% and 21-day marks you set."
The change log
- **The Rate Simulator**: you type an occupancy per room type and see what your rules would do with it.
The Rate Simulator

Your property system's occupancy report and MAYA's sellable occupancy answer different questions.

**Cloudbeds:** Cloudbeds' headline occupancy keeps blocked rooms in the total, so a night with 3 rooms blocked and 8 of 12 sold reads 67% there. MAYA does not read Cloudbeds' room blocks at all. It subtracts only the rooms you enter as out of service on the **PMS** tab, and then reads 8 of 9, which is 89%. If the two numbers disagree, that is usually why.
Read [Occupancy looks wrong](@98) for a checklist.

If none of the room types a rule measures has any sellable rooms on a night, occupancy is unknown for that night, and an occupancy condition is treated as not met. This happens when every measured type is fully out of service, or when the only measured types do not count as rooms. The rule stays quiet rather than firing on nothing. A room type with 0 sellable rooms is skipped, and the rest of the measured types are counted as usual.

To build it, follow [Raise prices when you are nearly full](@73).

**Not yet** · There is no way to tell MAYA about room blocks or allotments held in your property system. Enter them as rooms out of service on the **PMS** tab instead.

Booking window is the number of days until the stay, on your property's own calendar. Tonight is 0, tomorrow night is 1. **Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 7 covers tonight and the next six nights. The count moves every day, so a night slides into a rule's range as it gets closer.

For each night your rules run on, booking window is the stay date minus today's date, in whole days. "Today" is the calendar date at your property, in your property's time zone, at the moment of the check. A night 30 days away has a booking window of 30. Tonight has a booking window of 0.

The condition has nothing to do with when a guest booked. It is about how far away the night is right now.

The rule builder's label is **Booking window (days to stay)**. Its fields are **Compare** (**Greater than** or **Less than**) and **Threshold**, which starts at 7. A threshold with a decimal is rounded to whole days when you save.

Less than 7 covers tonight and the next six nights.

Comparisons are strict, so:

| You set | Nights covered |
|---|---|
| **Less than** 7 | Tonight and the next six nights (0 to 6) |
| **Less than** 3 | Tonight, tomorrow and the night after (0 to 2) |
| **Less than** 1 | Tonight only (0) |
| **Greater than** 45 | Nights 46 days away and further, up to the edge of the 60-night window |
| **Greater than** 0 | Every night except tonight |

Your rules run on tonight and the next 59 nights, so a **Greater than** rule reaches at most night 59. The one exception is a price you type further out: saving it runs your rules once on every night up to it. Read [How rules run](@39#the-window).

Tonight is night 0 and is inside every check. A rule set to **Less than** 1 acts on tonight alone. Past nights are never priced and never re-priced, so a night stops being touched the moment your property's date moves past it.

"Last minute" has two rows: **Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 3, and **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Less than** 50. It lowers the price by 15%.

- Tomorrow night, 7 of 20 rooms booked (35%): 1 day away and under half full, so the rule fires. Standard drops from $150 to $127.50.
- Tomorrow night, 14 of 20 booked (70%): 1 day away but not under half, so nothing happens.
- Five nights away, 4 of 20 booked (20%): quiet, but 5 is not less than 3, so nothing happens yet. In three days, if it is still quiet, it will.

A booking window rule is a standard rule: it holds its change while both conditions are true and takes it off when either stops. If a late booking lifts tomorrow night to 55%, the 15% cut comes off on the next check.

Read [Price last-minute nights differently](@76) for the click-by-click recipe.

When a booking window rule acts, the change log says how far away the night was and which mark it crossed:

- **Less than** 7: "It had 5 days to go, past the 7-day mark you set."
- **Greater than** 21: "It had 30 days to go, beyond the 21-day mark you set."
- With occupancy on the same rule: "It was 95% full with 17 days to go, past the 90% and 21-day marks you set."

"Past" for a less-than rule means the night has come inside your mark. "Beyond" for a greater-than rule means it is still further out than your mark.

The note under the **Rate Simulator** tab's **Stay date** field says that the date sets the days to arrival. The days are counted from your property's date, not from your computer's, so a property in the United States sees the same number the real run would see, even late in the evening.

Days are counted on your property's calendar. A check that runs at 11 pm on Friday at the property still treats Friday night as night 0. A check that runs at 12:30 am on Saturday treats Saturday night as night 0 and Friday as past.

MAYA's day changes at midnight in your property's time zone, whatever time your night audit runs. MAYA does not read your property system's business date. After midnight, the night before is in the past: MAYA no longer prices it or sends a price for it, and you cannot type a price for it either. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@105).

Booking speed compares how many bookings a night received in the past day, week or month with how many similar nights in your own history had received at the same point before arrival. A booking with several rooms counts once. Seven levels run from **Stalled** to **Surging**. You pick one, and your rule fires when the night reads that level or beyond.

In the rule builder, choose **Booking speed (recommended)** in the **Metric** dropdown. Three fields appear:

- **Speed**: the level, from **Stalled** to **Surging**. It starts at **Faster Than Normal**.
- **Measured over**: the window MAYA counts in, **Past day**, **Past week** or **Past month**. It starts at **Past week**.
- **Then waits (advanced)**: how long the rule leaves a night alone after acting on it. It starts at **1 week**.

There is no **Compare** dropdown for this condition. The level you pick already says which way the rule looks (see [Picking a level](#picking-a-level)).

A "?" beside **Measured over** opens a panel titled **How booking speed works**. It says in a few lines what this page says in full, with the same example: about 5 bookings expected, 1 reads much slower, 5 or 6 normal, 10 much faster.

Say your rule measures **Past week**, and the night is Friday, November 13, 2026, 40 days away. MAYA counts the bookings made for that Friday in the past 7 days. Then it takes similar Fridays from your own history and counts what each of them received in the 7 days when it, too, was 40 days away. Their average is the night's "expected" count.

It is Sunday, October 4, 2026. Five similar Fridays at The Harbour Inn received 4, 6, 5, 3 and 7 bookings over those 7 days. The highest and the lowest are set aside, and the average of 4, 6 and 5 is 5. So 5 bookings are expected. Here is how the Friday reads, depending on how many bookings it received itself:

| Level, as shown on screen | Reads as | With 5 expected |
|---|---|---|
| **Stalled** | far fewer bookings than similar nights had | 0 |
| **Much Slower Than Normal** | half or fewer | 1 |
| **Slower Than Normal** | clearly fewer | none at this size |
| **Normal** | about the same | 2 to 8 |
| **Faster Than Normal** | clearly more | 9 |
| **Much Faster Than Normal** | twice as many or more | 10 to 17 |
| **Surging** | far more | 18 or more |

Small gaps read as Normal on purpose. With 5 expected, anything from 2 to 8 is inside the ordinary ups and downs, which is why **Slower Than Normal** never shows at this size. The smaller the numbers, the bigger the gap has to be, so a rule stays quiet on small numbers rather than firing on them.

With fewer than five similar nights to compare with, the reading stays within one step of Normal: **Slower Than Normal**, **Normal** or **Faster Than Normal**. That is always the case on a night near a holiday (see [Picking a level](#picking-a-level)).

This is a comparison with your own past. Booking speed does not say how many bookings a night will end up with, and it does not look ahead. It says whether the bookings so far are ahead of or behind what your own similar nights had at the same point.

Expected 5, received 9, with 5 similar nights: Faster Than Normal.

[Booking speed in detail](@35) has the fine print: exactly which bookings count on each property system, how expected is worked out, and the exact lines between the levels for other numbers. [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36) explains how the similar nights are chosen.

You pick one level. The rule fires when the night reads that level or anything beyond it on the same side of Normal.

| You pick | The rule fires when the night reads |
|---|---|
| **Stalled** | Stalled only |
| **Much Slower Than Normal** | Much Slower Than Normal or Stalled |
| **Slower Than Normal** | Slower Than Normal, Much Slower Than Normal or Stalled |
| **Normal** | Normal only |
| **Faster Than Normal** | Faster Than Normal, Much Faster Than Normal or Surging |
| **Much Faster Than Normal** | Much Faster Than Normal or Surging |
| **Surging** | Surging only |

The rules list shows the condition as "booking speed at least Much Faster Than Normal (past week), then waits 2 days". A level below Normal reads "at most". **Normal** shows no word at all.

The five starter rules, the same five for every property that gets them, show how the levels are meant to work together. Read [Your starter rules](@27) for what each one says on the review screen and why a property may not have them.

| Starter rule | Speed | Measured over | Then waits | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Slow-date rescue | Much Slower Than Normal | Past month | 1 week | Decrease 15% |
| Slow-date trim | Slower Than Normal, exactly (see below) | Past month | 1 week | Decrease 7% |
| Warm-date bump | Faster Than Normal | Past month | 3 days | Increase 10% |
| Hot-week surge | Much Faster Than Normal | Past week | 2 days | Increase 25% |
| Sudden-spike catcher | Surging | Past day | 1 day | Increase 25% |

Slow-date trim is the one exception to the table above. It fires on exactly **Slower Than Normal**, so that Slow-date rescue handles anything slower. A rule you build yourself cannot do that: picking **Slower Than Normal** in the builder fires on Slower and everything below it.

At a small property, or on nights far out, expected is small and the strongest levels are rarely reached. **Faster Than Normal** and **Slower Than Normal** fire more often, because they include everything beyond them.

Holiday nights are a firm limit. A night near one of the 17 US holidays is compared with at most 3 past nights, one a year, so it only ever reads **Slower Than Normal**, **Normal** or **Faster Than Normal**. Rules set to **Much Faster Than Normal**, **Surging**, **Much Slower Than Normal** or **Stalled** do nothing on those nights, roughly 64 to 70 a year. That includes three of the starter rules: Slow-date rescue, Hot-week surge and Sudden-spike catcher. For holiday nights, use a rule set to **Faster Than Normal** or **Slower Than Normal**. [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36#holidays) lists the holidays and their stretches.

Two recipes use the one-step levels: [Cut prices on nights booking slowly](@74) and [Catch a sudden rush](@75).

**Past day**, **Past week** and **Past month** are 1, 7 and 30 booking dates, counting today. A short window reacts to a burst within a day and is noisy on quiet nights. A month smooths the count and reacts later. The starter rules use **Past day** to catch a spike, **Past week** for a surge, and **Past month** for the slow-date rules and the warm-date bump.

The similar nights are always read over the same length of window, at the same distance from arrival, so a long window never compares a month of this night with a week of another.

After a booking speed rule adjusts a night, it leaves that night alone for the wait you chose: **1 day**, **2 days**, **3 days**, **1 week** or **2 weeks**. A rule saved before the choice existed waits 1 week. The wait is counted per night and per room type, in 24-hour periods from the moment the rule acted.

If the same rule also has a **Pickup count** condition with a longer lookback, the rule waits the lookback instead. The shorter options in the dropdown then say so, for example "(pickup holds it to 3 days)". A stronger rule can still step in while this one waits. Read [How rules run](@39) for the wait in full, including which rule fires when several are true.

A booking speed rule fires, its change stays on the price, it waits, and it can fire again if the night still reads that level. The second time, it does not count the same bookings again.

Once a night has been raised, a rule that raises counts only the bookings that arrived after that raise, whichever booking speed or pickup rule made it. A rule that cuts counts from the night's last cut in the same way. The similar nights are read over the same days of their own curves, so the comparison stays fair.

So your booking speed rules never stack two raises on the same burst of bookings. A stronger booking speed rule adds its raise on top only when the bookings since the first raise read that fast on their own. A price you type starts the count over: after the rule's wait, it counts its whole window again.

MAYA now counts three days: the bookings that arrived after Monday's raise, then all of Tuesday's and Wednesday's. It compares them with the same three days of each similar Friday's curve. The rule fires again only if those three days on their own read Much Faster Than Normal.

If it does, the change log says: "Bookings came in much faster than normal in the 3 days since this night was last raised: 6, against the 2 a night like this usually gets in those days."

[Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts) covers the rest: the day of the raise itself, raises made by rules you have since switched off, and the exact wording under **How did we know?**.

A raise made on **Faster Than Normal** or above comes off by itself when enough of the bookings behind it cancel: when the bookings still on the books from the stretch the rule counted are back down to what a night like it usually gets. Each raise is tested on its own numbers, and never in the run that made it.

The change log then says the rule "stopped applying an earlier 25% raise here: enough of the bookings behind it cancelled." This line appears only when another change is still on that night. If the raise was the only one, the night returns to its base price and the change log lists nothing for it.

While the rule is switched off, its raises stay on the price and are not checked for cancellations. Switch it back on and the check resumes.

A booking speed rule stays quiet on a night when:

- **There is not enough history.** No similar nights could be found and there was nothing nearby to read momentum from, so the condition is never true. A quiet rule leaves nothing in the change log. You see this only when something else changed that night's price while the rule was switched on: **How did we know?** then begins "We do not have enough history yet to say what would be normal for this night", and says no booking speed rule was allowed to act there. A property with no bookings in MAYA yet shows nothing at all until the first bookings arrive. Read [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36#not-enough-history).
There is not enough history

- **The price is already at its limit.** A rule that raises does not fire on a night already at the room type's ceiling, and a rule that cuts does not fire on a night already at its floor. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
The price is already at its limit
- **You chose to stop it on that night.** When the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner asked, you clicked **Stop for this night**. **Let it run again** on the **Rules** tab undoes that.
You chose to stop it on that night

- **The night has no price to start from**, for example a rate of 0 in Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations. Such a night is left unpriced, and no rule acts on it. (On Mews, MAYA does not read your rates, so a 0 there has no effect.)
The night has no price to start from

- **The rule is switched off, or does not change that room type.** Its switch on the **Rules** tab reads **Off**, or the room type is not in its **Change** list. Rules have no dates or days to set, so a rule that is on covers every night in the window.
The rule is switched off, or does not change that room type
- **Every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room.** The rule measures nothing, so it cannot read a pace. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).
Every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room
- **The rule is waiting.** Its wait on that night and room type is not over.
The rule is waiting
- **Another rule holds the night.** A stronger rule that is still true keeps a weaker one from firing under it. Read [How rules run](@39).
Another rule holds the night

- **The night is near a holiday and the rule asks for a stronger level.** A holiday night reads at most **Faster Than Normal** or **Slower Than Normal**, so a rule set further out never fires there.

Occupancy rules and booking window rules work from day one. Booking speed needs your history, which is why MAYA imports it as soon as you connect. Read [The history import](@23).

In the Rate Simulator, the **Booking speed** dropdown starts at **Not enough history**, which keeps booking speed rules quiet in the same way. Read [Trying rules out in the Rate Simulator](@43).
The night is near a holiday and the rule asks for a stronger level

**Does a wedding or a group booking count as lots of bookings?** No. A booking with several rooms counts once for booking speed, while all its rooms still count for [sellable occupancy](@32). Rooms booked as separate reservations, for example guests booking from a room block, count as separate bookings. Read [What is counted](@35#what-is-counted).
Does a wedding or a group booking count as lots of bookings?

**Is booking speed a forecast of demand?** No. It describes how a night has booked so far, against your own similar past nights at the same point, and says nothing about where the night will end up. There is no forecast of occupancy or demand anywhere in MAYA. Read [No forecasts](@0#no-forecasts).
Is booking speed a forecast of demand?

**Why did it raise a night that is still empty?** Booking speed does not look at how full the night is. On a quiet night far out, 2 bookings against an expected 0 reads **Much Faster Than Normal**, and a raise rule fires. That is what a far-out rush looks like, for example after a concert is announced months ahead, and it clears the same checks as everything else. If you want raises only on busy nights, add a **Sellable occupancy (%)** row to the same rule, so both must be true.
Why did it raise a night that is still empty?

**Why did it cut a night that is nearly full?** For the same reason. A cut rule reads the pace of recent bookings, not the total. A nearly full night that received nothing this month, against similar nights that received 6, reads slow. Add an occupancy row (**Less than** 70, say) to keep cuts away from full nights.
Why did it cut a night that is nearly full?

**Why does MAYA say Faster Than Normal from only two bookings?** Because similar nights had almost none at the same point, so 2 is a real change. With five or more similar nights behind it, 2 bookings against an expected 0 reads **Much Faster Than Normal**. With fewer than five, the reading stays one step from Normal, at **Faster Than Normal**.
Why does MAYA say Faster Than Normal from only two bookings?

**Why does it say Normal when we got far more bookings than usual?** Usually one of three things. The difference is still small in bookings (with 3 expected, anything from 1 to 5 reads Normal). The bookings came in before a booking speed or pickup rule last raised the night, and the rule now counts only the ones since. Or the similar nights were as busy at the same point, so this night is keeping pace rather than running ahead. **How did we know?** in the change log shows the counts.
Why does it say Normal when we got far more bookings than usual?

**Can I see a night's booking speed before a rule acts on it?** Not yet. The calendar does not show it, and the **Rate Simulator** works on a night you make up, so it counts nothing. A real night's reading shows under **How did we know?** in the change log, under a change on that night, when a booking speed rule was checked there.

To watch for a level while your property is in simulation, add a rule set to the level you are curious about. When a night reads that level or beyond, the rule fires there (unless a stronger rule holds the night), and the change log shows the reading under the change without sending anything. The change log keeps about the last 50 minutes on screen, so look soon after. Delete the rule before you go live. Read [When the reading shows](@35#when-the-reading-shows).
Can I see a night's booking speed before a rule acts on it?

**Can bookings that later cancel move my prices?** For a while, and only inside your floors and ceilings. Every booking still on the books counts for booking speed, whatever channel it came from, so bookings that are made and later cancelled (speculative bookings, test bookings or fake ones) can make a raise rule fire before they cancel. On Mews, enquiries and optional reservations count too. Here is what keeps that in check:

- A cancelled booking leaves the count on the next read, as if it had never been made. It never counts as a negative, so making and cancelling bookings cannot make a night read slower than it would have.
Can bookings that later cancel move my prices?

- Every price stays between the room type's floor and ceiling. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
- Once a rule has adjusted the same night three times, the amber banner asks you whether it should keep going.

Read [When a price change comes off](@40) for every case.

Both count what a night gained recently. Booking speed compares the count with your own past nights, so the same three bookings can read as a rush in February and as normal in August. Pickup count compares with a fixed number you type, and counts room nights rather than bookings. That is why the builder labels them **Booking speed (recommended)** and **Pickup count (advanced)**. Read [Pickup count (advanced)](@37) for when a fixed number is the right tool.

**Not yet** · You cannot see a night's booking speed on the calendar or before a rule acts on it. You cannot move the lines between the levels, change the checks that hold small gaps at Normal, or change how many similar nights are used.

This page is the fine print behind booking speed. A booking counts once on each night it covers, dated the day it was made, and only in the room types a rule measures. Expected is the average of what up to eight similar past nights received over the same stretch, with the highest and lowest set aside. Small gaps read as Normal on purpose, so a rule stays quiet on small numbers.

Start with [Booking speed](@34) if you have not read it. It covers what you choose in the builder, the seven levels and which one to pick.

For each night in the window, MAYA counts the bookings made for that night during the stretch your rule measures. Five things set what goes into the count.

**One booking counts once.** A booking is one reservation for one night, however many rooms it holds. A 20-room reservation is 20 booked rooms for [sellable occupancy](@32) and one booking for booking speed.

It counts as one booking on each night it is booked for, and as one booking again whenever one of those nights is later used as a similar night for another date. If a room is added to that reservation a week later, it is still one booking, dated when it was first made, so the added room never reads as a new booking. Rooms booked as separate reservations, for example guests booking from a room block or allotment, count as separate bookings. MAYA does not read room blocks.
One booking counts once

**The date is the booking date.** A booking counts on the day your property system recorded it, not on the day of the stay. **Past day** counts bookings dated today. **Past week** counts bookings dated today and the six days before it. **Past month** counts today and the 29 days before it. "Today" is today on your property's own calendar, so a reading taken at 12:10 am has almost nothing in **Past day** yet.
The date is the booking date

**Each night counts its own bookings.** A three-night stay is one booking on each of its three nights, because each night is priced on its own. That is why one booking can turn up in the count for two different nights: it is a booking for both, not two bookings on one.
Each night counts its own bookings

**An extension keeps the booking's date.** When a guest extends a stay, or a booking's dates are changed in your property system, the added nights belong to the same booking, dated when it was first made. They count as booked rooms for sellable occupancy on the next read, but they are usually too old to count in **Past day** or **Past week**. This is the same in Cloudbeds, ThinkReservations and Mews. If the extra nights are booked as a new reservation instead, that is a new booking, dated the day it was made.
An extension keeps the booking's date

**Only the room types the rule measures are counted.** A rule that measures Standard and Deluxe counts bookings in those types and no others. A room type you have unticked as a room is never counted. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

When a guest cancels, your property system stops reporting the booking and it leaves the count on the next read. It is not counted as a negative. Every booking counts the same whatever channel it came from: there is no way to count only direct bookings.
Only the room types the rule measures are counted

**ThinkReservations:** ThinkReservations reports each room booking inside a reservation on its own. MAYA groups them back into one booking by the reservation, so a reservation with three rooms is one booking. Every booking counts except cancelled bookings and no-shows. The booking date is the reservation's creation date, on your property's calendar.

**Mews:** A Mews reservation is one room, so each reservation is one booking, including each reservation in a group. Every Mews reservation counts, including enquiries and optional (tentative) and requested ones. Only cancelled reservations are left out. Read [Which bookings count](@14#which-bookings-count). The booking date is the reservation's creation date, on your property's calendar.

A count on its own says little. Three bookings in a week is a rush for a quiet Tuesday in February and a worry for a Saturday in August. So MAYA compares the count with what similar nights in your own history had received by the same point.

Each night is compared with up to eight similar past nights from the last three years: the same weekday (or, near a holiday, the same position around it) and the same time of year. A night near a holiday has 3 similar nights at most, one from each year. [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36) explains how they are chosen and what happens when there are too few.

Expected is the average of those counts. Once there are five or more similar nights, the single highest and the single lowest are dropped before averaging, so one odd night cannot swing the number. The result is kept to two decimals, so expected can be a fraction, such as 0.4 for a quiet night far out. On screen it reads "almost none" when it is under 1, and is rounded to a whole number otherwise.

A similar night that has no bookings anywhere in your history is treated as unknown, not as zero, and is left out of the average. A night that has history but nothing in the stretch is a real zero and stays in.

The smaller the numbers, the bigger the gap has to be compared with what is usual before a night reads anything but Normal. With 5 expected you need 9 to read **Faster Than Normal**, nearly double. With 20 expected you need 27, about a third more. The outer levels, **Stalled** and **Surging**, need a bigger gap still. With fewer than five similar nights to compare with, the reading stays within one step of Normal. That is always the case near a holiday.

These checks can only pull a reading towards Normal, never away from it. When one of them held a reading back, **How did we know?** says so in one of three lines. Each is quoted here only far enough for you to find it:

- "The raw numbers leaned away from Normal": the gap was too small for this many bookings, so the level stays Normal.

- "We found only a few": there were fewer than five similar nights, so the level stays within one step of Normal however strong the numbers look. A reading built from momentum (see [similar nights](@36#momentum-when-nothing-matches)) always counts as one similar night, so it always stays within one step.

**Example: The exact lines, for the curious**

MAYA divides the count by expected, with expected treated as at least 0.5 for the division. At least 1.25 times expected reads Faster Than Normal, at least 2 times Much Faster, at least 3.5 times Surging. The slow side mirrors it: 0.8 times or less is Slower, half or less Much Slower, 1 in 3.5 or less Stalled.

How many bookings a night needs, in the window, to read each level. Computed from the lines and checks above, with five or more similar nights behind the expectation.

| Expected | Stalled | Much Slower | Slower | Normal | Faster | Much Faster | Surging |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (a night far out) | never | never | never | 0 or 1 | never | 2 or 3 | 4 or more |
| 1 | never | never | never | 0 to 2 | never | 3 or 4 | 5 or more |
| 3 | never | 0 | never | 1 to 5 | never | 6 to 10 | 11 or more |
| 5 | 0 | 1 | never | 2 to 8 | 9 | 10 to 17 | 18 or more |
| 10 | 0 to 2 | 3 to 5 | never | 6 to 14 | 15 to 19 | 20 to 34 | 35 or more |
| 20 | 0 to 5 | 6 to 10 | 11 to 13 | 14 to 26 | 27 to 39 | 40 to 69 | 70 or more |

Two things in the table are on purpose. At small expectations some levels can never be reached: with 1 expected, one missing booking is inside the ordinary ups and downs, so the night cannot read slow at all. And with fewer than five similar nights, every "Much" cell and both ends collapse to **Faster Than Normal** or **Slower Than Normal**. Nights near a holiday always read this way, because they never have more than 3 similar nights.

**Example: Where the Friday lands**

Take the Friday from [Booking speed](@34#how-a-night-reads), with 5 expected from five similar Fridays. In the past week it received 9 bookings, 1.8 times the usual, and a gap of 4 is big enough at this size. Five similar nights is enough for the full range. The level is **Faster Than Normal**.

With 10 bookings instead of 9, twice the usual, the level is **Much Faster Than Normal**. With 18, 3.6 times the usual, it reads **Surging**. With 1 booking, a fifth of the usual, the first reading would be Stalled, but a gap of 4 is not enough for the outermost level, so it steps in to **Much Slower Than Normal**.

Once a night has been raised, a rule that raises counts only the bookings that arrived after that raise, whichever booking speed or pickup rule made it: the rest of the day it was raised, then every day since. That includes a raise made by a rule you have since switched off, and even a raise that later came off after cancellations. A raise stops counting only when a price you type takes it off, or when you delete the rule that made it.

A rule that cuts counts from the night's last cut in the same way: the rest of the day of the cut, then every day since. Raises and cuts keep separate starting points. A raise or cut made by a standard rule (occupancy or booking window) does not change what a booking speed rule counts.

The similar nights are read over the same days of their own curves, so the comparison stays fair. They had no change that day, so for them the first day counts in full. A pickup rule is different: it always measures its whole lookback, so it can add a raise on bookings a booking speed rule has already acted on.

**Example: What the change log says after a re-count**

In the Hot-week surge example on [Booking speed](@34#after-the-rule-acts), the rule raised Standard for Friday, November 13, 2026 on Monday, October 12 and counted again on Wednesday, October 14. For the similar Fridays, those three days fell 30 to 32 days before arrival, and their Monday counts in full.

When only the day of the raise has been counted so far, the change log says "later on the day this night was last raised" and ends with "in a day" instead of "in those days". The second sentence under **How did we know?** then begins "Later that day".

Two things follow:

- **Another rule can act on the same day.** If a raise rule fired on the night earlier today, another raise rule can still act on that night today, but only on the bookings that arrived after the raise. A raise earlier the same day never keeps a booking speed rule quiet on its own, unless the rule that raised earlier ranks above it and still reads true over its full window. That rule then holds the night through its wait (read [How rules run](@39#which-one-fires-when-several-match)).
Another rule can act on the same day

- **A price you type starts the rule over.** Typing a price on a night takes the rules' changes off it. A booking speed rule then waits its wait from the moment you typed, and after that it counts its whole window again, including bookings from before your price. Read [Setting a price yourself](@49).
A price you type starts the rule over

You cannot see a night's booking speed on the calendar. The reading appears in the change log, under **How did we know?**, under a price change on that night when at least one of your booking speed rules was checked there in that run.

- A rule that is switched off, or that you stopped on the night, is not checked.
- A rule that is waiting on every room type it changes that night is checked only when another booking speed or pickup rule is ready to fire on one of them.
- A night whose price did not change shows no reading.

The **Rate Simulator** lets you pick a level for a made-up night, but does not count anything.

A rule that measures every room type ticked as a room reads the whole hotel's history. A rule that measures only some types (Standard alone, say) gets its own counts over the same similar nights, shared with every other rule that measures the same set.

Two things follow. A room type that started selling only last year has no data before its first sale, so it has fewer similar nights and its reading more often stays within one step of Normal. And a small set has a small expected, so small gaps keep the reading at Normal more often. That is by design: a rule on a small set fires less often rather than wrongly.

If a rule on two Suites seems too quiet, widen what it measures: tick **Change prices on different room types**, measure your whole property and change only the Suites.

Each night is compared with up to eight similar past nights from the last three years: the same weekday (or, near a holiday, the same position around it) and the same time of year, skipping closures and any dates you have set aside. A night near a holiday has at most three, one a year. Away from holidays, with too few, MAYA widens the search a step and says so. With none, it reads booking momentum from nearby nights instead. With nothing at all, booking speed rules stay quiet on that night.

A booking speed rule compares a night's recent bookings with what similar nights had received at the same point before arrival. The comparison is only as good as the nights behind it. This page is about how those nights are chosen, in the order MAYA tries things. Read [Booking speed](@34) for what is done with them.

Which past nights count as similar does not depend on the rule, so every rule uses the same ones. What each rule counts on those nights depends on the room types it measures.

You never see the similar nights while a rule is being checked. You see them afterwards, in the change log, and only under a price change: open **How did we know?** under a change on that night, then **Why did you expect that?**, then **Show me the nights you compared**. **How did we know?** is there only when at least one of your booking speed rules was checked on that night in the same run. A rule that is off, or that you stopped on the night, is not checked. A rule that is waiting on every room type it changes that night is checked only when another booking speed or pickup rule is ready to fire on one of them. Read ["How did we know?" explained](@47).

For a night that is not near a holiday, MAYA looks for at least 4 similar nights and keeps at most 8. They come from the three years before the night being priced, up to yesterday. A night near a holiday works differently: it is compared with that holiday in each of the three previous years, so it has 3 similar nights at most (read [Holidays](#holidays) below). Some nights are never used, whatever else is true of them:

- nights inside a closed period you confirmed during the review
- nights you have set aside as not a fair comparison
- a window of dates around a yearly event, once your reports from 2 different years agree on it

Read [Closed periods and set-aside dates](#closed-periods-and-set-aside-dates) below.
For a night that is not near a holiday, MAYA looks back through your history, most recent first, in up to three steps. It takes the next step only when the ones before have found fewer than 4 nights.

1. **First, the same weekday in the same season.** MAYA steps back 7 days at a time and keeps the nights inside the same season, never a night near a holiday. The reasons you read are "a Friday", "your Peak Season" (or "your Year-Round"), and "earlier this year", "recently", "about a year earlier", "2 years earlier" or "3 years earlier".
First, the same weekday in the same season

2. **If fewer than 4 are found, the same kind of night in the same season.** Friday and Saturday are weekend nights, and every other night is a weekday night, so a Saturday can stand in for a Friday. The reason reads "a Saturday, similar to a Friday".
If fewer than 4 are found, the same kind of night in the same season

3. **If there are still fewer than 4, the same weekday at a nearby time of year.** Any night on the same weekday within 45 days of the same point in the year counts, whatever the season. The reason reads "a nearby time of year".

When your history is too thin to show seasons, or shows none, the whole year is one season called "Year-Round". The first step then keeps the nearest same-weekday nights, whatever the time of year.

When more than 8 qualify, the best 8 are kept: nights from the first step before the second, the second before the third, and within a step the nearest in time first.
If there are still fewer than 4, the same weekday at a nearby time of year

If the second or third step was needed, the list under **Why did you expect that?** includes a line that starts "Strict matching found too few usable nights". It means the first step found fewer than 4 nights, so looser matches were added, and it is why a Friday can be compared with a Saturday. The rest of the line asks you to keep that in mind when you weigh how much to trust the reading. To check, open **Show me the nights you compared** and look at the dates. If one of them was not a normal night, set it aside with **Not a fair comparison?** (read [Setting a date aside](@48)).

Every night is read over the same stretch of its own booking curve as the night being priced. A Saturday 40 days out is compared with how each similar Saturday was booking when it was 40 days out.

**Example: A Friday in November at The Harbour Inn**

It is Sunday, October 4, 2026 and the night is Friday, November 13, 2026. The first step goes back a week at a time from the night. Fridays later in October 2026 have not happened yet, so the first candidates are Fri, Oct 2 2026, then Sep 25 and so on, kept only when they fall in the same season as November 13. Then come Fridays from the same season in 2025 and 2024, such as Fri, Nov 14 2025 and Fri, Nov 15 2024. The Friday after Thanksgiving is skipped every year. If fewer than 4 Fridays qualify, the second step adds Saturdays from the same weeks, and the drill-down says so.

Weekends are Friday and Saturday nights. Sunday is a weekday night. MAYA uses that in two places: in the second step of the search, where a Saturday can stand in for a Friday, and in how seasons are read, which watches how Friday and Saturday nights book against the rest of the week (see [Seasons](#seasons) below). Holidays use a wider weekend of their own: a holiday that falls on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday counts as a weekend holiday (see [Holidays](#holidays) below).

**"Our weekend is Thursday and Friday nights. Can MAYA use a different weekend?"** No. There is no setting for which nights are your weekend. Away from holidays, the first and third steps of the search always compare a night with the same weekday, so your Thursdays are compared with Thursdays and your Saturdays with Saturdays. Only the second step, used when the first finds fewer than 4 nights, groups nights into weekend (Friday and Saturday) and weekday (Sunday to Thursday). There a Thursday can be compared with a Monday, and a Friday with a Saturday. Every date on this page is a date on your property's own calendar. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@105).

A night inside a holiday's stretch is compared by its position around the holiday, not by its weekday. The Saturday after Thanksgiving is compared with the Saturday after Thanksgiving in each of the last three years, whatever the dates were. Thanksgiving always falls on a Thursday, so there the weekdays line up.

For a holiday on a fixed date, the position around it is the same date every year, so the compared nights usually fall on other weekdays. Saturday, December 26, 2026 (the day after Christmas) is compared with Friday, December 26, 2025, Thursday, December 26, 2024 and Tuesday, December 26, 2023. All three are kept. The fixed-date holidays are New Year's Day, Valentine's Day, St. Patrick's Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Halloween, Veterans Day and Christmas.

A year in which the holiday fell on a similar part of the week scores higher, and the reason reads "similar weekend placement". The parts of the week are a weekend (a holiday on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday), a Monday or Thursday, and midweek (a Tuesday or Wednesday). The score only changes the order of the nights, never which ones are used. When the matching night sits nearer a different holiday that year, it is kept but ranked lower, with the reason "also Father's Day that year".

Under **Why did you expect that?** a line starts "This night sits in the orbit of Thanksgiving". It means the night is near Thanksgiving, so it was compared with the same position around Thanksgiving in earlier years, not with the same calendar date. Above it, a holiday night also gets the weekday line, such as "We only compared against other Saturday nights". Around a holiday that moves with the weekday, such as Thanksgiving, that is true. Around a fixed-date holiday it is not accurate, because the compared nights usually fall on other weekdays. Go by the holiday line and by the dates under **Show me the nights you compared**. There, each night's reasons give the year and the position, for example "Thanksgiving 2025; 2 days after the holiday; similar weekend placement".

| Holiday | Days before | Days after |
|---|---|---|
| New Year's Day | 1 | 1 |
| Martin Luther King Jr. Day | 3 | 1 |
| Valentine's Day | 1 | 1 |
| Presidents' Day | 3 | 1 |
| St. Patrick's Day | 1 | 1 |
| Easter | 2 | 1 |
| Mother's Day | 2 | 0 |
| Memorial Day | 3 | 1 |
| Father's Day | 2 | 0 |
| Juneteenth | 1 | 1 |
| Independence Day | 2 | 2 |
| Labor Day | 3 | 1 |
| Indigenous Peoples' Day | 3 | 1 |
| Halloween | 1 | 1 |
| Veterans Day | 1 | 1 |
| Thanksgiving | 1 | 3 |
| Christmas | 1 | 7 (through New Year's Eve) |

A night inside two stretches belongs to the nearer holiday.

Nights that are not near a holiday are never compared with nights that are. A night near a holiday is compared only with the same holiday in earlier years, with one exception: if none of those past holiday nights has any bookings (for example in your first year), the night is read from momentum, which uses the ordinary nights around it. MAYA does not read weather, event listings or any holiday feed. Its only inputs are your own bookings.

**"My hotel is outside the US. Do Thanksgiving and July 4 still change how my nights are compared? Can I turn them off?"** Yes, they apply to every property, and there is no switch to turn them off. In a year, roughly 64 to 70 nights fall inside one of these stretches. Each of those nights is compared with the same position around the same US holiday in earlier years, and your ordinary nights are never compared with them. When none of those past holiday nights has any bookings, for example in your first year, the holiday night is read from momentum instead, which uses the ordinary nights around it. For a holiday on a fixed date, such as Independence Day (July 4), that means the same dates in earlier years, whatever weekday they fell on. For one that moves, such as Thanksgiving (the fourth Thursday of November), it means the matching days around it.

**Not yet: Your own holidays** · There is no screen to add a holiday, a school break or a local festival, or to switch a US holiday off, and none is read from anywhere. The workaround is to set the dates aside. Open a change on the **Change Log** tab, click **How did we know?**, then **Why did you expect that?**, then **Show me the nights you compared**, and click **Not a fair comparison?** under the night. Choose the first reason in the list (the one for a holiday) and the scope **This happens every year around this time**. Once you have reported it from 2 different years, that window is skipped every year. Read [Setting a date aside](@48).

"Season" here means a stretch of your year that books differently from the stretches around it: busier or quieter, with stronger or weaker weekends, or filling earlier or later. Your seasons come straight from your own booking history. They are worked out again each time your rules run, so you never set or maintain them (and cannot edit them).

How seasons are read, in plain terms:

- The input is how many rooms each past night in the last three years sold, and how early it filled. Price is never used, so your own past pricing cannot bend the result.
- MAYA needs booked past nights on at least 120 different days of the year (about four months). With less, the whole year is one season called "Year-Round".

Seasons are named by their level: "Peak Season", "Low Season" and "Shoulder Season" (or "June Shoulder Season" when there are several). When the levels are close and the seasons differ in shape rather than size, they are named by their place in the year instead: "June Season" or "June to August Season".

You will only ever meet a season name inside an explanation, in a line such as "We stayed inside the same demand season your history shows: Peak Season (June 10 through August 31)." or "We stayed inside the same demand season your history shows: Year-Round (January 1 through December 31)." There is no seasons page and no season setting. Each change log entry keeps the season it used at the time. So an older entry can name a season, or season dates, that no longer match today's. New readings work seasons out again from your current history each time your rules run.

**Not yet: Your own seasons** · You cannot see your seasons in one place, define a season, rename one or move its edges. Seasons are worked out again from your bookings each time your rules run, so a change in how you book changes them with no work from you. If a past stretch is skewing them (a renovation, a one-off event), set those dates aside: any date you set aside, with any scope, stops counting toward your seasons from the next run. Choose **This should also change how our seasons are read (advanced)** only when the same stretch repeats every year. Once reports from 3 different years agree, the whole window around it is left out of your seasons every year.

Sometimes no similar night can be found at all: a room type that has never sold at this time of year, a holiday night whose earlier years have no bookings, a night far outside your history, or a night crowded by set-aside dates. MAYA does not invent a number. It makes one simpler reading, called momentum: how the nights near this one are filling right now, compared with how the same nights were filling a year ago.

In short: if the nearby nights have 6 bookings between them now, against 5 at the same point a year ago, they are filling about 20% faster. If this night itself had 4 bookings at this point a year ago, expected is 4 raised by 20%, about 5.

**Example: The exact steps, for the curious**

- It looks at the 10 nights on either side of the night being priced, keeping only nights that are today or later, not near a holiday, and not set aside. It needs at least 2 of them.

- Each of those nights is paired with the same night 364 days earlier (52 weeks, so the weekday lines up) at the same distance from arrival, when that year-ago night has history and is usable. The paired nights' bookings now, added together, divided by the same nights' bookings a year ago is the momentum ratio, held between 0.15 and 6.
- With no pairs, or when the year-ago nights had no bookings in that stretch, the ratio is 1. In the second case the drill-down still reads "Those nights are filling at about the same pace as a year ago.", because there was nothing a year ago to measure a change against.

Under **Why did you expect that?** the list opens by saying that the night had no usable comparable nights in your history, so MAYA read your recent booking momentum instead. It goes on with lines such as "3 nearby nights could be paired with their counterparts from last year." and "Those nights are filling about 20% faster than they were a year ago.", and ends with "A momentum read is fuzzier than a direct comparison", a reminder to treat it as a best effort, not a measurement. The year-ago nights behind a momentum read are listed under **Show me the nights you compared**, and you can set any of them aside like any other comparison.

When there are no similar nights and momentum has fewer than 2 usable neighbouring nights, the reading is "not enough history". A booking speed condition is never true on such a night, so booking speed rules do nothing there. Occupancy and booking window rules are unaffected.

A rule that stays quiet leaves nothing in the change log, because the change log lists price changes. So you only see this reading when something else changed that night's price (another rule, a price you typed, or on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations a rate change in your property system) while a booking speed rule was switched on. Then **How did we know?** begins "We do not have enough history yet to say what would be normal for this night", and goes on to say that no booking speed rule was allowed to act there.

This happens on a night whose nearby nights are nearly all holiday nights or set-aside dates. It also happens on a property with no bookings in MAYA at all, where no reading is made anywhere, so nothing is shown at all, not even under **How did we know?**. A night far outside your history, or a room type that started selling recently, still gets a reading: when none of its similar nights has bookings, it is read from booking momentum, capped at Faster or Slower. On a new property it clears on its own once the first bookings arrive.

Booking speed rules also stay quiet when none of the room types a rule measures still counts as a room. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

Two kinds of night are never used as a comparison:

- **Closed periods.** Stretches of at least 14 days with no bookings, with normal bookings on both sides, that you confirmed as a closure on the review after the import ("Were you closed ... ?"). Read [Checking what MAYA found](@26).
Closed periods

- **Dates you set aside.** Any night you flagged with **Not a fair comparison?**. It is left out from the next run. Say it happens every year and, once reports from 2 different years agree, a window of 5 days either side is skipped every year. Read [Setting a date aside](@48).

Undoing a set-aside date makes it comparable again on the next run.
Dates you set aside

- "We only compared against other Friday nights" (the line goes on to say why weekdays are not mixed). This line appears even when the criteria were relaxed, when a Saturday may have been used, or the night is a holiday. The list under **Show me the nights you compared** shows the weekdays actually used.
- "We stayed inside the same demand season your history shows: Peak Season (June 10 through August 31)."
- A line starting "Strict matching found too few usable nights" (only when the second or third step was needed, as described above).
- "Closed periods and any dates you have told us were not normal are left out of the comparison entirely."

For a night read from momentum: a first line saying that this night had no usable comparable nights in your history, so MAYA read your recent booking momentum instead, followed by "Momentum means: how nights near this one are filling right now, compared to how the same nights were filling at this time last year." and the counts behind it.
