For a night with not enough history: "There was not enough history to form any expectation, so no rule was allowed to act on booking speed for this night."

After the night has already been raised: "Once a night has been raised, rules that raise count only the bookings made after that raise, whichever rule made it, the rest of that day included, and read the nights it is compared with over the same days." Here "whichever rule" means any booking speed or pickup rule: a change made by an occupancy or booking window rule does not count.

Pickup count is how many room nights (one room for one night) or how much revenue a night gained in the last 1, 3 or 7 days: what is booked now minus what was booked when the window opened. Cancellations pull it down, so it can be negative. It compares with a fixed number you type. Booking speed is usually the better choice, because it compares with your own similar nights instead.

About every five minutes, each time your rules run, MAYA records what is booked for each of the next 60 nights (tonight and the next 59). A pickup rule compares two of those records, over the room types the rule measures:
- **now**: what is booked for the night this time your rules run
now

- **when the window opened**: what was booked 1, 3 or 7 days ago

Pickup is now minus then. For pickup, each room on each night counts one: a four-room booking for one night is 4 room nights of pickup. That is different from [booking speed](@34), where the same booking counts once.

**Pickup measures** sets the unit:

- **Room nights (units)**: the number of booked rooms, rounded to a whole number.
- **Revenue (currency)**: the sum of each booked room night's current rate, as your property system reports it, in your property's currency, to the cent. Nothing is converted.

A booking counts the same whatever channel it came from. There is no way to count only direct bookings.
when the window opened

Choose **Pickup count (advanced)** in the **Metric** dropdown. The row shows:

- **Compare**: **Greater than** or **Less than**. Comparisons are strict: **Greater than** 5 means 6 or more room nights, not 5 exactly.
- **Threshold**: the number of room nights, or the amount, starting at 5. It must be 0 or more. Decimals are kept.
- **Lookback window**: **1 day**, **3 days** or **7 days**, starting at **3 days**.
- **Pickup measures**: **Room nights (units)** or **Revenue (currency)**, starting at room nights.

The window opens exactly 1, 3 or 7 days before the moment of the check, in hours, not at midnight on your property's calendar. A check at 3:05 PM with a 3-day lookback compares with the most recent record taken at or before 3:05 PM three days earlier (never one taken after that moment). That is different from booking speed, whose windows are whole booking dates. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@105).

When more rooms cancel than book, pickup is below zero. A rule set to **Less than** 0 fires on nights that are losing bookings. A rule set to **Greater than** anything does not fire on them. The threshold itself cannot be negative.

**Example: A pickup rule at The Harbour Inn**

"Quick pickup" is **Pickup count (advanced)** **Greater than** 4 over **3 days**, measuring room nights, and raises Standard, Deluxe and Suite (the builder's default: the types that count as rooms) by 10%.

Three days ago the Saturday had 8 rooms booked across Standard, Deluxe and Suite. Now it has 14. Pickup is 6, which is more than 4, so the rule fires and raises Standard, Deluxe and Suite by 10%. It then waits 3 days (its lookback) before it can act on that night again.

A pickup rule needs a record from when the window opened. When there is none for one of the measured room types, or the most recent one is more than 12 hours older than that moment, the condition is false and the rule does nothing on that night. This happens:

- **On a newly connected property, or for a new room type.** MAYA starts keeping records the first time your rules run. A 3-day lookback can only be measured once your rules have been running for 3 days.
On a newly connected property, or for a new room type
- **After a long gap in runs**, for example a connection that was down for days. Once your rules run again, the rule measures again after a full lookback.
After a long gap in runs
- **When every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room, or has been switched off in MAYA.** There is nothing to record. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).
When every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room, or has been switched off in MAYA

- **On the furthest nights of the 60-night window.** Records are written only for nights inside the window, so a night has to have been inside it for the whole lookback. A 1-day rule cannot act on night 59, a 3-day rule on nights 57 to 59, and a 7-day rule on nights 53 to 59. Each night becomes measurable as it moves closer.

Records are kept for at least 14 days, whatever lookback your rules use. That is a week more than the longest lookback, 7 days, so a 7-day rule has what it needs once it has run for a week, except on those furthest nights.
On the furthest nights of the 60-night window

A pickup rule works like a booking speed rule. When it fires, its change stays on the price. It then waits its own lookback window before it can fire on that night and room type again, so a 3-day rule fires at most once every 3 days on a night. That way a window never reaches back past the rule's own last fire, and the rule never counts the same booking twice.

A rule that has both a pickup row and a booking speed row waits the longer of the two, and the **Then waits (advanced)** dropdown says so beside the shorter options. With a 7-day lookback they read "(pickup holds it to 1 week)". With a 3-day lookback they read "(pickup holds it to 3 days)". Read [How rules run](@39).

**Good to know** · A raise made by a pickup rule also counts as the night's last raise for your booking speed rules. After it, a booking speed rule that raises counts only the bookings that arrived after that raise, starting the same day, so your booking speed rules do not raise again on the same burst. It does not work the other way round: a pickup rule always measures its whole lookback, so it can add a raise on bookings a booking speed rule already acted on. Read [Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts).

A raise made by a **Greater than** pickup rule comes off by itself when cancellations bring the booked rooms for that night, over the measured room types, back down to where the window opened when it fired. A raise made by a **Less than** rule was not caused by bookings, so cancellations never undo it. A cut never comes off by itself. While the rule is switched off, its raises stay on the price and are not checked for cancellations. Switch it back on and the check resumes. Read [When a price change comes off](@40).

On screen, pickup always says "bookings". Read it as room nights (or your amount, for a revenue rule).

On the **Rules** tab a pickup condition reads "Pickup above 5 bookings" or "Pickup below 2 bookings". In the change log it reads "9 bookings arrived in the last 3 days, past the 4-booking mark you set.", where 9 is room nights (a two-room booking for the night is 2) and "the last 3 days" is the lookback. When a rule measures different room types from the ones it changes, the sentence names them: "9 Standard and Deluxe bookings arrived in the last 3 days, past the 4-booking mark you set."

The **Rules that keep adjusting** banner names the unit: "Pickup over the last 3 days came to 6 room nights, against the 4 you set." A revenue rule shows money there.

Both look at what a night gained recently. The difference is what the count is compared with. Pickup's fixed number is right for some nights and wrong for others: 5 room nights in 3 days is a rush for a quiet Tuesday and nothing special for a Saturday in peak season.

|  | Pickup count | Booking speed |
|---|---|---|
| Compares with | a fixed number you type | what similar past nights had received by the same point |
| Counts | room nights, or revenue | bookings (a booking with several rooms counts once) |
| Window | 1, 3 or 7 days, in hours | past day, week or month, in booking dates |
| Needs history | no, only records from the window start | yes, similar past nights |
| Same count in February and August | reads the same | reads differently, against each season's own pace |

Pickup suits a fixed line you already trust, a property with no history yet, or a rule that should watch revenue. Booking speed suits everything else, which is why the rule builder labels it **Booking speed (recommended)**.

When you click **Get suggestions from my data** on the **Rules** tab, MAYA may suggest removing a pickup rule that one of your booking speed rules already covers (it measures and changes at least the room types your pickup rule does, on at least the same days and dates). The suggestion says the pickup rule reacts to a fixed booking count that the booking speed rules now cover with pace awareness, and that keeping both would stack two price reactions on the same demand. You choose **Remove it**, **Turn it off, keep it** or **Leave it running**. Nothing changes unless you accept. Read [Getting suggestions later](@29).

The **Rate Simulator** has a **Picked up** box per room type, in rooms. A revenue rule is tested by valuing those rooms at the base price you typed for that room type.

**Not yet** · The rule card does not show a pickup rule's lookback or whether it measures room nights or revenue. Put both in the rule's name when you build it, for example Pickup 3 days revenue. Pickup cannot be measured in hotel days, only in 24-hour periods.

Tick **Change prices on different room types** and the rule watches one list of room types (**Measure**) and prices another (**Change**). Only room types that count as rooms can be measured. Anything can be changed. Unticked, one list does both.

In the rule builder, the room types field starts as one list, **Apply to room types**, with every type that counts as a room ticked. Under it is a checkbox, **Change prices on different room types**, with a "?" beside it that opens a panel titled **Measure and change**:

- "You watch occupancy, pickup and booking speed on the Measure room types."
- "When the rule fires, you change prices on the Change room types."
- "Unticked, one list does both."

Tick it and the field splits in two:

- **Measure**: the room types the rule reads its numbers from. Only room types that count as rooms are offered here, because occupancy and booking speed are only ever counted over rooms.
- **Change**: the room types whose prices the rule changes. Every active room type is offered, including ones tagged "not a room".

- A room type that does not count as a room is never measured, on its own or alongside rooms. If you select only the Meeting Room, the rule still prices it but measures nothing. Any sellable occupancy, booking speed or pickup count condition on it can never be true, so the rule never fires. Only a booking window condition, which reads no room types, still works.
- To price a type on its own bookings, tick it as a room on the **PMS** tab (which also counts it in your occupancy and in the rooms you are billed for), then build the rule. There is no other way to measure it.
- With the checkbox unticked and nothing selected: "Select at least one room type."
- With the checkbox ticked and **Measure** empty: "Pick at least one room type to measure."
- With the checkbox ticked and **Change** empty: "Pick at least one room type to change."

- **Sellable occupancy** is rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell, over the measured types only. A rule measuring Standard reads Standard's occupancy, which can differ from the day card's whole-hotel figure. Read [Sellable occupancy](@32).
Sellable occupancy

- **Booking speed** counts bookings in the measured types only, on the night being priced and on every similar past night. A measured set smaller than the whole hotel gets its own counts, shared by every rule that measures the same set. Read [Booking speed on part of the hotel](@35#booking-speed-on-part-of-the-hotel).
Booking speed
- **Pickup count** adds up room nights (or revenue) gained over the measured types. Read [Pickup count (advanced)](@37).
Pickup count

- **Booking window** reads no room types. It is the same number of days for every type.

For occupancy and pickup, one reading serves every room type the rule changes. A booking speed rule can read each changed room type separately, because each one counts from its own last raise or cut. Either way, the rule fires and waits separately for each changed room type, so Suite and Deluxe can each be on a different step of the same rule. Read [How rules run](@39).
Booking window

On the **Rules** tab, the **Room Types** column normally lists the types the rule changes. When the rule measures something different, it reads "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite". Only measured types that count as rooms are named there, because those are all the rule measures.

The **Rate Simulator** shows the same thing beside the rule under **Rules in play**.

When a rule measures different room types from the ones it changes, its change log sentences say so:

- "Standard and Deluxe were 92% full, past the 90% mark you set."
- "Standard and Deluxe bookings came in faster than normal this past week: 9, against the 5 a night like this usually has by now."

**Example: Suites that follow your standard rooms**

The Harbour Inn has 12 Standard rooms, 6 Deluxe and 2 Suites. Two Suites are too few to read on their own, so Priya builds "Suites follow": **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Greater than** 80, **Increase the rate** 10%, checkbox ticked, **Measure** Standard and Deluxe, **Change** Suite.

On a Friday with 11 of 12 Standard and 5 of 6 Deluxe booked, the measured occupancy is 16 of 18, which is 89%. The rule fires and raises the Suite from $300 to $330. The Suites' own bookings play no part.

"Busy nights, Deluxe only" measures Standard, Deluxe and Suite and changes only Deluxe. Whole-property occupancy above 80% raises Deluxe alone. Standard and Suite keep their prices.

**Example: A meeting room priced from the rooms**

"Busy nights, Meeting Room" measures Standard, Deluxe and Suite and changes only the Meeting Room. The Meeting Room's price follows how full the hotel is, and its own bookings never count towards occupancy.

A rule reads its numbers only from room types that count as rooms. What happens with the rest:

- **A rule saved with a mixed list** (Standard and the Meeting Room, say, before you unticked the Meeting Room on the **PMS** tab) keeps pricing every type in its **Change** list, but the Meeting Room drops out of what it measures. The change log tells you: "That 95% leaves out Meeting Room."
A rule saved with a mixed list

- **A rule whose measured types have all been unticked** measures nothing. Any sellable occupancy, booking speed or pickup count condition on it can never be true, so it stops firing. It stays **On** on the **Rules** tab, with no warning. A standard rule's change comes off. A booking speed or pickup rule's earlier changes stay where they are.
A rule whose measured types have all been unticked

- **A rule whose measured types have all been switched off in MAYA** (during the review) stops running. Any price change it had already made on the types it changes stays in place, as if the rule were switched off. To clear it, delete the rule or type a price for those nights. Removing a room type in your property system does not switch it off in MAYA, so the rule keeps measuring it. [Room types and rooms out of service](@51) says what happens to a removed room type in each system, and [Contact support](@110#your-property-system) lists what you can ask us to change.

A booking window reads no room types, so a rule whose only condition is a booking window keeps working when every type it measures has been unticked as a room.
A rule whose measured types have all been switched off in MAYA

**Good to know** · Whether a room type counts as a room is set on the **PMS** tab with the **Counts as a room** checkbox. Unticking a type takes it out of occupancy, booking speed, the revenue per room behind the calendar colours and the room count you are billed for. It can still be priced. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@51).

**Not yet** · A rule cannot measure a room type that does not count as a room, on its own or alongside rooms. To price a meeting room or a court on its own bookings, tick it as a room on the **PMS** tab. To price it from how full the hotel is, **Measure** your rooms and **Change** it. A rule also cannot measure one set of room types for occupancy and a different set for booking speed. Two rules, one for each, act separately, and their changes stack.

About every five minutes MAYA reads your bookings, then checks every rule on every night from today to 59 days out, for each room type. Standard rules (occupancy, booking window) switch on while their condition holds and off when it stops. Booking speed and pickup rules fire, keep their change on the price, wait, and can fire again. Percent changes compound, fixed amounts add, and the result stays between the floor and ceiling.

A cycle is one run of MAYA for your property. It comes round about every five minutes. Each cycle:

1. reads your bookings from your property system
2. refreshes your own rates when they are due (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations)
3. runs every rule on every night in the window, for every room type
4. sends the prices that changed, if your property is live (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations)

On Mews, a cycle reads your bookings and runs your rules, and that is all. Your own rates are not read and nothing is sent, live or not. Read [Nothing is sent to Mews](@14#nothing-is-sent-to-mews).

Typing a price on the calendar runs the rules again at once, without waiting for the next cycle. If a cycle cannot read your bookings, it prices nothing and sends nothing, and the next cycle tries again.

- Tonight is night 0 and is always priced.
- A night 59 days away is the last one in a scheduled cycle. A night 60 or more days away is not in it, which is why a rule usually fires 59 days out and not 61. The night comes into the window a day later and is priced then.
- Past nights are never priced or re-priced. Once your property's date moves past a night, every change on it is left as it was.
- A price you type 60 or more nights ahead is saved now and sent when the night enters the window. Saving it also runs your rules once on every night from tonight to the last night you typed, so a rule can act on a night 90 days out then. Those changes count in **Fired**, appear in the change log and stay on the far nights until each night enters the window and is checked again. Nothing is sent for a night until it is inside the 60-night window.

The **How rules behave** panel on the **Rules** tab shows two short animations of this. The panel calls the second kind pickup rules. Booking speed rules work the same way, so these docs say "booking speed and pickup rules".

|  | Standard rule | Booking speed or pickup rule |
|---|---|---|
| Conditions | Only sellable occupancy and booking window | Has a booking speed or pickup count row (with or without the others) |
| How it acts | Switches on when its condition starts to hold, keeps one change on the price while it holds, switches off when it stops | Fires, and the change stays on the price when the condition stops holding |
| Same night twice | Never. One change while the condition holds | Yes. After its wait, if still true, it fires again and the changes stack |
| When the change comes off | As soon as the condition stops holding | A raise made on **Faster Than Normal** or above, or on a pickup count **Greater than** 0 or more, comes off when enough of the bookings behind it cancel (read [When a price change comes off](@40)). Other raises and all cuts never come off by themselves |

The panel's own summary says the same: a standard rule follows the night as it is now and takes its change off when its condition stops holding, while a booking speed or pickup rule acts on each moment its condition holds and keeps that change.

2. your own rate for the night, read from your property system
3. the rate of the newest booking for that night and room type
4. the base saved for the night on the last run

On Mews, your own rates are not read and a rate changed in Mews is never read back, so the base is a price you typed in MAYA, else the newest booking's rate, else the base saved on the last run. Read [Where a night's starting price comes from](@14#where-a-nights-starting-price-comes-from).

If your system shows the night's rate as 0 (a closed night, for example) and you have not typed a price, MAYA leaves the night unpriced. No booking speed or pickup rule fires on it, nothing is sent and the calendar shows a dash for its price. This applies on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, where MAYA reads your rates.

Standard rules still switch on and off on that night as their condition starts and stops holding, and each switch-on counts in **Fired**. So once the night has a rate, any standard rule already on there applies straight away, and the change log shows it from then.

If your system sends no rate at all for the night (blank, not 0), MAYA uses the next starting point in the list above instead. And a 0 you typed yourself is a real price: a comp night. Read [Setting a price yourself](@49).

For each night and room type:

- **Activate.** The conditions hold and the rule was not active there. The change goes on the price. This counts as one fire in the **Fired** column.
Activate
- **Hold.** The conditions still hold. Nothing changes, and the rule does not fire again.
Hold

- **Deactivate.** The conditions stop holding. The change comes off and the price goes back.

So a cancellation that drops a night from 82% to 78% takes a "Greater than 80" raise off on the next cycle. A late booking that lifts it back above 80 puts it on again, and that counts as another fire.
Deactivate
- **Fire.** The conditions hold, the rule is not waiting on that night and room type, and it wins the competition (below). The change goes on the price. One fire.
Fire

- **Wait.** The rule leaves that night and room type alone for its wait: the **Then waits (advanced)** setting for a booking speed rule (1 day to 2 weeks, starting at 1 week), the lookback window for a pickup rule, and the longer of the two for a rule with both. The wait is counted in 24-hour periods from the fire.
Wait

- **Read again.** When the wait is over, the rule reads the night again. A booking speed rule counts only the bookings made since the night was last raised (for a rule that raises) or last cut (for a rule that cuts), whichever booking speed or pickup rule did it, rules you have switched off included. The similar nights are read over those same days. If that reads the level the rule asks for, it fires again and the change stacks on the earlier one.
Read again

- **Tell you at three.** Once a rule has adjusted the same night three times, an amber banner asks you whether to keep going. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@42).

The change log shows a repeat as "Then "Hot-week surge" raised it another 25%, from $250.00 to $312.50."

A 2-day wait after a raise on Monday afternoon: the rule reads the night again on Wednesday afternoon and counts only the bookings made since the raise, Monday afternoon through Wednesday, against the same 3 days of similar nights.

**Example: A 2-day wait after a Monday fire**

The starter rule "Hot-week surge" is **Much Faster Than Normal** or faster over **Past week**, waits **2 days**, raises 25%. It fires on the Saturday's price on Monday afternoon.
Tell you at three

If Monday's burst was the whole story, the bookings since the raise read Normal and the price holds at one raise. If bookings keep coming, it raises again on Wednesday, waits until Friday, and so on. At three raises on that night, MAYA asks you.

**"My rule's wait is over and the night still reads faster, so why did it not act again?"** Because the whole-window reading you see in an older log entry includes the bookings the rule already acted on. After a fire, the rule only counts what arrived since. If those bookings alone do not read faster, it does nothing. That is by design: one rule never stacks two raises on the same bookings.
"My rule's wait is over and the night still reads faster, so why did it not act again?"

At most one booking speed or pickup rule fires on a given night and room type in one cycle. When two or more are true and not waiting, MAYA ranks them. The first step where they differ settles it:

1. Starter rules come before rules you build, in this order: Sudden-spike catcher, Hot-week surge, Warm-date bump, Slow-date rescue, Slow-date trim. Every rule you build ranks the same at this step.
2. Next, the rule with more conditions comes first.
3. Next, for two pickup rules with the same **Compare**, the stricter threshold comes first (**Greater than** 6 before **Greater than** 4).
4. Next, the bigger move in money on that night's base comes first (10% of $200 is $20, which beats $15).
5. Last, the older rule comes first.

You built "Busy week", a booking speed rule that raises. On Monday, October 12, 2026, it and the starter rule "Hot-week surge" are both true on Saturday, November 14, 2026. Starter rules rank first, so Hot-week surge raises the Saturday and "Busy week" does not.

Hot-week surge then waits 2 days. On Tuesday "Busy week" is true on the Saturday again, but Hot-week surge still reads true over its full past week and ranks higher, so it holds the night: "Busy week" cannot fire there while Hot-week surge waits.

Before ranking, a rule is dropped for that night when it could not move the price: a raise on a night already at its ceiling, a cut already at its floor, a percent on a price of 0, or any raise on a night you set to 0.

Standard rules do not compete. Every standard rule whose condition holds applies.

For each night and room type, MAYA starts from the base price and applies:

1. every active standard rule change, in a fixed order that is not the order you made them (this only matters when a percent rule and a fixed-amount rule both hold on the same night)
2. every open booking speed and pickup fire, in the order they were made
3. the floor and ceiling

Percent changes multiply: $200 raised 10% is $220, and 25% on top of that is $275, not $270. Fixed amounts add: $200 plus $25 is $225. The result is rounded to cents, and that is the only rounding there is. There is no setting to round to whole numbers or to make prices end in 9. For a price such as $199, type it yourself. Rules that fire later still stack on it and round to the cent. If it would go above the room type's ceiling, the ceiling is published. If it would go below the floor, the floor is.

You can only type a price inside the floor and ceiling, or 0 for a comp night. If a limit changes later, a price you already typed stays as you typed it. Rules on top of it are held between the limits, stretched to include your price. Say Standard's floor was $60 when you typed $70, and you later raised the floor to $80. Your $70 stays. A cut rule can take it no lower than $70, and a raise can go up to the $300 ceiling.

$200, up 10% to $220, then up 25% to $275. The $300 ceiling is not reached, so $275 is published.

Now a festival night, with Standard's rate at $290 and its ceiling at $300: "Busy nights" asks for $319. The change log adds "That would have gone past your $300.00 ceiling for Standard, so it stopped there." and $300 is published. "Hot-week surge" does not fire on Standard at all, because a raise cannot fire on a night already at its ceiling. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).

Your rules check every night in the window about every five minutes, but a night's price changes only when something changes it, and it is sent to your property system only when it changes (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, once you are live). On a quiet property, hours can pass with nothing sent. Guests do not see a price bouncing every five minutes.

What can move a night's price, and how often:

- **A standard rule** changes it once when its condition starts to hold and once when it stops. A booking window rule starts to hold as the night gets closer. An occupancy rule on a night that hovers around its line can switch on and off as bookings arrive and cancel.
A standard rule
- **A booking speed or pickup rule** changes it at most once per wait. At most one of these rules fires on a night and room type each cycle.
A booking speed or pickup rule
- **Three adjustments** by the same rule on the same night bring the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner, which asks whether it should keep going.
Three adjustments

- **You**, when you type a price, and **your own rate**, when it changes in your property system.

So a night can still change more than once in a day when bookings come and go, but never only because five minutes passed.
You

Everything above happens separately for each room type the rule changes. Waits run per night and room type. Floors and ceilings are per room type. So a rule can fire on Deluxe and not on Standard on the same night: Standard may still be waiting, sitting at its ceiling, or measured differently. The **Fired** column counts every time the rule acted, once per night and room type each time.

Turning a rule off freezes what it has done: its changes stay on the price and nothing new happens. Deleting a rule undoes everything it did from the next cycle. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@41).

The **Change Log** tab lists every pricing run that changed a price, with the chain of rules and running prices for each room type and night, so stacking is visible. Under a booking speed change, **How did we know?** opens the counts behind it. Read [The change log](@46) and ["How did we know?" explained](@47).

**Careful** · In simulation everything above runs and is written to the change log, but nothing is sent. After you go live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, changed prices go to your property system every cycle. Nothing is sent to Mews. Read [Simulation mode](@53).

A standard rule's change comes off when its condition stops holding. A booking speed raise comes off when enough of the bookings behind it cancel. A cut never comes off by itself. Your typed price takes earlier changes off that night. Deleting a rule undoes everything it did. Turning a rule off undoes nothing.

A standard rule (only **Sellable occupancy (%)** and **Booking window (days to stay)** rows) holds one change on a night and room type while its condition holds, and takes it off on the first cycle where it does not. Nothing else is needed.

**Example: A cancellation at The Harbour Inn**

"Busy nights" raises 10% when a night is more than 80% full. Friday is 17 of 20 booked (85%): Standard is $165. Two guests cancel, so Friday drops to 15 of 20 (75%). On the next cycle, about five minutes later, the raise comes off and Standard goes back to $150. If a new booking lifts Friday over 80% again, the raise goes back on.

The **How rules behave** panel on the **Rules** tab animates exactly this: "Next evaluation: conditions no longer match. The rule turns off and the price reverts to $200."

A booking speed or pickup raise stays on the price after the rule fires. It comes off on its own in one case: enough of the bookings behind it cancel. Which test applies is fixed at the moment the raise fires.

| The raise came from | It comes off when |
|---|---|
| Booking speed at **Faster Than Normal** or above, with more bookings than expected in its window | the bookings still on the books from the days it counted are back down to what a night like it usually gets over those days |
| Pickup count **Greater than** a number of 0 or more, with bookings up over its window | the rooms booked for the night, over the room types the rule measures, are back down to where they were when the window opened |

The bar is deliberately high. One or two cancellations out of a real rush do not undo a raise. Each stacked raise is tested on its own numbers. A raise is never taken off in the same cycle that made it, never while its rule is switched off, and never once the rule measures a different set of room types from the one it measured when it fired.

**Example: Four cancellations, then three more**

On Monday, October 12, 2026, "Hot-week surge" raised Saturday, November 14, 2026 by 25%, after 12 bookings arrived in a week when a night like it usually gets 5. Four of those 12 cancel: 8 are still on the books, more than 5, so the raise stays. Three more cancel: 5 are left, back to the usual 5, so the raise comes off on the next cycle.

When another rule or a price you typed is still on that night, the change log says: "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: enough of the bookings behind it cancelled. When the raise was the only change on the night, the price goes back to the base and the change log lists nothing for that night. The calendar shows the price it is at now.

A cut never comes off by itself, whatever happens to the bookings. That is by design: a cut that switched off the moment a booking arrived would have undone the thing that brought the booking in. If bookings have recovered and you want the price back up, type the price you want on the calendar, or delete the rule, which undoes every cut it made.

**"Bookings recovered, so why did the cut not come off?"** Because a cut is only ever undone by you. A cut rule can keep cutting the same night after each wait, down to your floor. After three cuts the amber banner asks whether it should keep going, and until you answer, it does. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@42).

When you type a price for a night and room type on the calendar:

- every booking speed and pickup change already on that night and room type comes off ("this night's price was set by hand" in the change log)
- every standard rule change already there is held: the rule stays on, so it does not fire again on the same trigger, but it stops moving the price until its condition next changes
- your number becomes the base, and rules that fire later stack on top of it
- a booking speed or pickup rule that already existed waits its wait from the moment you saved, then reads its whole window again

Read [Setting a price yourself](@49). Clearing your price hands the night back: held standard rules move the price again, but the booking speed and pickup changes that came off stay off.

**Careful: Typing a price is the quickest undo** · If a price looks wrong and you want it fixed now, type the price you want. It is saved at once. If you are live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations it is sent right away or on the next cycle, about five minutes later (the screen says which). A night more than 59 nights ahead is sent when it enters the 60-night window. A 0 is not sent, and nothing is sent to Mews. Read [Undo a price change](@66).

Today there is no edit control for a rule. The one change you can make in place is accepting a "Tune ... ?" suggestion after **Get suggestions from my data**, which moves the occupancy threshold of a standard rule. From the next cycle the rule checks every night against the new threshold, so a night that no longer meets it loses the change, and a night that now meets it gains one.
Once your property's date moves past a night, every change on it is left as it was and nothing touches it again. Past nights are never re-priced.

Deleting a rule removes every change it made, whether from a standard rule or a booking speed or pickup rule, from the next cycle. Every night it adjusted goes back to what the price would be if the rule had never run. The delete dialog says so and offers **Turn It Off and Keep Its Changes** beside **Delete Rule and Undo Its Changes**. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@41).

Turning a rule off undoes nothing: its changes stay exactly as they are.

| What happened | What you read |
|---|---|
| A standard rule switched off | If another rule or a typed price is still on the night, its next entry shows the price without the change, and no rule is named for the drop. If it was the only change, nothing: the night is back at its base and has no entry |
| A raise came off for cancellations | If another rule or a typed price is still on the night: "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: enough of the bookings behind it cancelled. If it was the only change, nothing |
| You typed a price | "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: this night's price was set by hand. Then a line naming who set it. |
| A rule was deleted | The next run prices without it. In older entries a deleted standard rule is called "Pricing rule" with no reason given, and a deleted booking speed or pickup rule's line is left out |

**"Why did the price go back to the base rate?"** One of: a standard rule's condition stopped holding, a raise came off after cancellations, you or a colleague cleared a typed price, or the rule was deleted. The change log lists a night only while a rule or a typed price is on it, so a night back at its base usually has no entry at all. Check the night's current price on the calendar. When another rule or a typed price is still on the night, its entry shows the price without the change, and names a raise that came off for cancellations.

**Not yet** · There is no undo button for one price change. The three ways back are: type the price you want on that night (now), delete the rule (undoes everything it did, everywhere), or stop the rule on that night from the banner if it has fired three times there (no more changes, and what it did stays).

Off freezes: the rule stops acting and the prices it already set stay exactly as they are. Delete undoes: every night it adjusted goes back to what it would have been. There is no edit yet. To change a rule, delete it and add it again.

Each rule on the **Rules** tab has a switch under **Status** that reads **On** or **Off**. Click it to flip it. There is no confirmation, and it takes effect from the next cycle. A rule cannot be switched **On** while 40 others are on (read [How many rules you can have](#how-many-rules-you-can-have)).

Off means the rule stops acting. It does not undo anything:

- a standard rule's change that was on a night stays on that night, and does not come off when the condition stops holding, because the rule is no longer being checked
- a booking speed or pickup rule's raises and cuts stay on the price, and its raises are not tested for cancellations while it is off
- on the day cards and in your property system, nothing moves

Turn the rule back **On** and it picks up from the next cycle. A standard rule that was holding a change then lets it go if the condition no longer holds.

**Good to know: A switched-off rule still marks where counting starts** · After a night has been raised, a booking speed rule that raises counts only the bookings made since that raise, whichever booking speed or pickup rule made it. A rule you switched off still made its raise, so it still marks where the other raise rules start counting on that night. Read [Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts).

- **Delete Rule and Undo Its Changes**: removes the rule and every change it made, from the next cycle
- **Turn It Off and Keep Its Changes**: switches the rule off and closes the dialog
- **Cancel**

The change log keeps its price entries, but older entries lose the deleted rule's reasons. A standard rule's move still shows, named "Pricing rule", with no sentence saying why. A booking speed or pickup rule's move is left out of those entries. Your answers to the rule's keeps-adjusting banner (the "Your answer" entries) are removed along with the rule. New entries show the price without it. Read [The change log](@46).

**Careful** · Deleting a rule changes prices. Every night the rule had adjusted is re-priced without it on the next cycle. On a live Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations property, those prices are sent to your system. On Mews they change in MAYA only. If you want the prices to stay where they are, turn the rule off instead.

If you want to keep the old prices in place while the new rule takes over, turn the old rule off instead of deleting it, and leave it off.

The one change that can be made in place is a "Tune ... ?" card after **Get suggestions from my data**, which moves the occupancy threshold of a standard rule. From the next cycle the rule checks every night against the new threshold, so a night that no longer meets it loses the change, and a night that now meets it gains one. Read [Getting suggestions later](@29) and [Change a rule](@71).

**Not yet** · You cannot edit, rename, copy or duplicate a rule, or copy one to another property. For all of these, add the rule again. A rule you build in the **Rate Simulator** arrives on the Rules tab switched off, which is handy for building the replacement before you delete the original.

The rules table has seven columns: **Name**, **Fired**, **Conditions**, **Room Types**, **Price Change**, **Status** and the **Delete** button. On a narrow screen it scrolls sideways.

**Order.** Most fired first, then rules that are on before rules that are off, then by name.
Order
**Filter.** The pills above the table, **All**, **Enabled** and **Disabled**, show every rule, only the ones that are on, or only the ones that are off.
Filter

**Fired.** How many times the rule has acted, counted once per night and room type. A dash means never. A "?" beside the heading explains that a booking speed or pickup rule can act on the same night more than once, and each time counts, and that a change that came off later still counts. So the count is usually higher than the changes you can see on the calendar now, and higher than the change log shows, which lists only the 40 biggest moves of each run.
Fired

**Conditions.** In words: "Occupancy above 80%", "Booking window below 7 days", "Pickup above 5 bookings", "booking speed at least Faster Than Normal (past week), then waits 1 week". Several are joined with a dot.
Conditions
**Room Types.** The types the rule changes, or "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite" when it measures different ones.
Room Types

**Price Change.** "+10%", "-15%", "+$25", "-$25". The sign in this column is always a dollar sign, whatever your property's currency. The amount is in your currency. The change log and the keeps-adjusting banner use your currency's own symbol.
Price Change
**Stopped on N nights.** An amber chip under the switch when you have told the rule to stop on some upcoming nights, with a "?" and a **Let it run again** link. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@42).

At most 40 rules can be **On** at once on a property. Rules that are **Off** do not count, and a rule saved from the **Rate Simulator** arrives Off. At 40, adding a rule shows "This property already has 40 active rules, which is the maximum." in red under the form, and the switch on an Off rule will not turn it On (no message appears, and the switch stays Off). Turn a rule off or delete one first.

Every occupancy or booking window rule whose condition holds applies, and their changes stack. Booking speed and pickup rules take turns: at most one fires on a night and room type per run. Read [How rules run](@39).

Revenue Managers, General Managers and Hotel Admins can switch and delete rules. A Viewer sees the switch and the **Delete** button, but clicking them changes nothing. Read [Roles: who can do what](@63).

The app does not show who added, switched or deleted a rule. If you need to know, [email us](mailto:info@modern-hospitality-solutions.com?subject=Who%20changed%20a%20rule) with the rule's name and roughly when.

The change log has no entry for adding a rule, switching it on or off, or deleting it: it shows only what those steps did to prices. The people the change log does name are whoever typed a price ("Priya set the base rate to $180.00.") and whoever answered the keeps-adjusting banner (the "Your answer" entries).

When a booking speed or pickup rule has adjusted the same night three times, an amber banner asks you: keep adjusting, or stop for this night. Until you answer, it keeps going. Stop means no more changes there, and what it already did stays. You can let it run again from the **Rules** tab.

A booking speed or pickup rule fires, waits, and can fire again on the same night. Each fire stacks on the last, so a night can climb (or fall) a long way on one rule. So at three, MAYA asks you.

The count is per rule, per night: the most fires the rule has on any one of that night's room types. Fires that are open count, and so do raises that were later taken off for cancellations. Fires that came off because you typed a price, or because the night passed, do not count. Only booking speed and pickup rules can reach three. A standard rule fires once per change of state.

The rule does not stop at three. It keeps firing after its wait, as usual, until you answer. The banner is your chance to say otherwise.

The banner appears a few minutes after the third change. It does not refresh by itself, so reload the page to see the latest.

It sits above the tab content on every tab, in amber, and opens straight with the rule's headline. One card per rule, rules A to Z. Each card has:

- **A headline.** "Hot-week surge" has raised Fri, Nov 13 2026 3 times. For several nights: "Slow-date rescue" has cut 4 nights, 3 times each (or "3 to 5 times each"). When a night's room types got different counts, it says "up to": "up to 3 times", or "up to 5 times each".
A headline
- **A consequence line.** "It keeps raising these nights until you stop it."
A consequence line

- **One block per night.** The night, then how often on each room type ("3 times on Standard and once on Deluxe"), then what the rule saw at its latest fire: "In the 7 days it measured, 9 bookings came in. A night like this usually has about 4 by then." or, for a pickup rule, "Pickup over the last 3 days came to 6 room nights, against the 4 you set."
One block per night

- **A limit line.** Where the price can go if the rule carries on: "If it keeps cutting, the price can fall to your $80.00 floor for Standard." When the limit is still the default: "Your ceiling for Suite is still MAYA's $99,999.99 default, so the price can climb that far." with a "?" and a link, **Ask MAYA for a ceiling** or **Ask MAYA for a floor**, which takes you to the **Rules** tab and its **Get suggestions from my data** button. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).

Prices in the banner use your property's currency symbol.
A limit line

**"Why does the alert show different counts per room type?"** Because waits, fires and limits run per room type. Standard may have been raised three times while Deluxe sat at its ceiling and was raised once.

"Hot-week surge" has raised Sat, Nov 14 2026 up to 3 times.
It keeps raising these nights until you stop it.

In the 3 days it measured, 6 bookings came in. A night like this usually has about 2 by then.

Under it, the two buttons, **Keep adjusting** and **Stop for this night**.
"Why does the alert show different counts per room type?"

**"Why does it say 3 days when my rule measures the past week?"** Once a night has been raised, a rule that raises counts only the bookings that arrived after the night's last raise, whichever rule made it. "Hot-week surge" waits 2 days, so at its third raise it counted the rest of the day of its second raise, then the two days after. A rule that cuts counts from the night's last cut in the same way. Read [Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts).
"Why does it say 3 days when my rule measures the past week?"

Each night has two buttons. The "?" beside them says:

- "Keep adjusting: the rule carries on as it is, and MAYA stops asking about that night."
- "Stop for this night: the rule makes no more changes on that night. A raise it already made stays, unless enough of the bookings behind it cancel." For a cut rule: "What it already cut stays."
- "A stopped night shows on the Rules tab, where you can let the rule run on it again; MAYA then asks about it again if the rule keeps adjusting it."
- "Either way, your other rules keep working on these nights" (the line goes on to mention editing the rule).

"I answered Stop but the price did not go back."

**"I answered Keep adjusting and changed my mind. How do I stop the rule on that night now?"** There is no undo for **Keep adjusting**. The night leaves the banner, it never shows under **Stopped on N nights**, and MAYA does not ask about it again for that rule. Three things you can do:
"I answered Keep adjusting and changed my mind. How do I stop the rule on that night now?"
- **Type a price** for that night on the calendar. The rule's changes there come off at once. After its wait, the rule can adjust your price again, and MAYA still does not ask.
Type a price
- **Turn the rule off** on the **Rules** tab. It stops on every night, and the changes it already made stay.
Turn the rule off
- **Delete the rule.** Every change it made comes off, on every night. If you add it again, it starts fresh, so the banner can ask about that night once more.
Delete the rule
**"Why did the price jump 50%?"** Two raises stacked, or three. The change log shows each step with its running price, and the banner shows how many times each room type has been raised.
"Why did the price jump 50%?"

When a card has more than one night, two whole-card buttons come first: **Keep adjusting on all N nights** and **Stop on all N nights**. The nights themselves sit behind a line naming the first three ("Fri, Nov 13 2026, Sat, Nov 14 2026, Sun, Nov 15 2026 and 4 more nights") with **Answer night by night** to open them and **Hide the nights** to close them.

Revenue Managers, General Managers and Hotel Admins. Anyone below that sees the same card with no buttons and the line "Only a Revenue Manager or above can answer this."

Messages you can meet when an answer fails: "That did not save. Try again in a moment." (try again), "Unknown alert." (the banner is stale, so reload the page), "You need manager access to do that."

The banner appears in simulation too, because the rules run and the fires are counted even though nothing is sent. Every sentence switches to the conditional: "would have raised", "It would keep raising these nights until you stop it.", "the price would climb to your $300.00 ceiling". Your answers work the same way.

**Let it run again** takes your answer off every night you stopped that rule on, in one click. The rule can act on them again from the next cycle, starting from the price it left. It asks you again only after three more adjustments on a night, not straight away.

**"MAYA says a rule is Stopped on 3 nights but I never answered anything."** A colleague did. The change log's "Your answer" entries name who.

Each answer is its own entry on the **Change Log** tab, headed "Your answer":

- "Priya stopped "Hot-week surge" on Sat, Nov 14 2026. The raises it already made stay, unless enough of the bookings behind them cancel." (a cut rule ends "What it already cut stays.")
- "Priya told "Hot-week surge" to carry on with 4 nights."
- "Priya let "Hot-week surge" run again on Sat, Nov 14 2026. It can start adjusting again from the next pricing run."

Someone whose name is not on file reads as "A manager". Up to 20 answers are shown.

If you type a price on a night that is in the banner, the rule's changes there come off, so the count falls under three and the night leaves the banner. If the rule later stacks its way back to three on your price, it asks again. That is only for a night still waiting for your answer: on a night you answered **Keep adjusting**, a typed price takes the rule's changes off, but MAYA does not ask again.

Stopping one rule on a night does nothing to your other rules. They keep measuring and changing that night as before.

**Not yet** · You cannot change the number three, turn the banner off, take back a **Keep adjusting** answer, or keep a rule off one night before it has adjusted it three times. Typing a price holds back the rules already on that night (their changes come off), but they can act on top of your price after their wait. To keep a night's price where it is, type the price and switch off the rules that would move it. Switching off stops a rule on every night, not only this one, so switch it back on once the night has passed.

Make up a night: a stay date, a booking speed level, and each room type's base price, occupancy and pickup. The simulator runs your real rules with the same maths a real run uses and shows what each room type becomes and why. Nothing is saved and nothing is sent. A test rule you build here can be saved to the **Rules** tab, switched off.

The **Rate Simulator** tab (the third tab on the dashboard) answers "what would my rules do to a night like this?" without waiting for such a night to come along. Its own words: "Make up a night and see what your rules would do to it. Nothing here is saved and no rate reaches your PMS." It adds that the maths is the same as a real run's, so what you see is what a real run would produce for these numbers.

Use it to check a rule before you build it, to see which of two rules would act, or to see why a price on the calendar is what it is. Everyone on the property can use it.

While it loads it reads "Loading this property's rooms and rules...". Before your first sync it says the property has no active room types yet, and asks you to connect a system and finish the import first.

Under **The night**:

- **Stay date**, starting 30 days ahead. The note under it says the date sets the days to arrival. They are counted from your property's date, not your computer's, so the number matches what a real run would see, and a booking window rule reads it.
- **Booking speed**, a dropdown with **Not enough history** and the seven levels: Stalled, Much Slower Than Normal, Slower Than Normal, Normal, Faster Than Normal, Much Faster Than Normal, Surging. It starts on **Not enough history**, and the note says booking speed rules then stay quiet, which is what a real run does when it cannot measure a pace. Pick a level to test a booking speed rule. A made-up night has no bookings to count, so the level you pick is taken as read.

One row per room type that counts as a room, with its room count under its name. Room types you have unticked as rooms are not here.

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Base price** | The price rules start from. It opens on the nearest price MAYA has published for that room type. With none published yet, it opens halfway between the floor and the ceiling when the ceiling is at most 10 times the floor, otherwise on the floor. |
| **Occupancy** | A percentage from 0 to 100, starting at 70. Beside it, "(8 of 12)" shows how many rooms that is, out of the full room count. Rooms out of service are not taken off here. |
| **Picked up** | Rooms gained over a pickup rule's lookback, starting at 0. A pickup rule that measures revenue values each one at the base price. |
| **Guardrails** | The room type's floor and ceiling, for reference. You cannot change them here. |

An occupancy rule reads occupancy across the room types it measures, added together. Two room types at 92% and 50% with 12 and 6 rooms read as 14 of 18, which is 78%. The rule checks its conditions once, on that one figure, so it fires on every room type it changes or on none of them.

Every rule on the property is listed with a checkbox, all ticked. Untick one to leave it out of the run. Beside each name:

- "ladder" or "event": the simulator's own words for the two kinds of rule. "ladder" is a standard rule (only occupancy and booking window conditions), which holds one change while its condition holds. "event" is a booking speed or pickup rule, which fires, keeps its change and can fire again after its wait. The rest of these docs say "standard rule" and "booking speed and pickup rules".
- "off" when the rule is switched off on the **Rules** tab
- "fires" when it fires on the night you have set up
- "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite" when the rule measures different room types from the ones it changes

- **Then** (**raise the rate** or **lower the rate**), **By** and **Unit** (**percent** or **dollars**).
- **Room types**, as pills, all on to start.

The draft runs in the table below as you edit it. "Until you press this, the rule exists only on this screen." **Discard test rule** throws it away.

**Save This Rule** saves it to the **Rules** tab switched off, and the screen reads "Rule Added to Rules Tab and Initialized as Disabled". Turn it on from the **Rules** tab when you are ready. Read [Try a rule before turning it on](@79).

The button stays greyed out until the draft has a condition, an amount and at least one room type. An amount of 0 (or a blank **By** box) cannot be saved: the save fails with an error. Type a real amount. Saving needs Revenue Manager access or higher: a Viewer who presses it sees an error.

**Good to know: No Measured over or Then waits here** · The test-rule builder has no **Measured over** or **Then waits (advanced)** fields. A booking speed test rule is saved with the defaults: **Past week** and a wait of **1 week**. A pickup test rule is saved with a 3-day lookback measuring room nights. For other settings, build the rule on the **Rules** tab instead. [The rule builder, field by field](@31) covers every field.

The results table has one row per room type: **Room type**, **Base**, **Becomes**, **Change** (the move in money, or a dash for none) and **Because**.

- **Becomes** is the price after every rule that fires and after the floor and ceiling. A "held at your floor" or "held at your ceiling" tag shows when a limit stepped in, and **Because** adds what the rules asked for, such as "Rules asked for $412.50."
- **Because** names each rule that fired, with "(currently off)" beside a rule that is off on the **Rules** tab, or reads "No rule fires on this night".

Under the table, **Didn't fire** lists each rule that did not fire and why:

| Reason | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Conditions not met (it saw 62% occupancy, 30 days out) | The night does not meet the rule's conditions. The numbers are what the rule read. |
| No occupancy for its signal room types | None of the room types the rule measures is in the table, so it has nothing to read. |
| Rule has no room types attached | The rule changes no room type. |
| Outside the rule's date window, or This day of the week is excluded | You will not see these for a rule you built in MAYA: every rule you build runs every day with no date window. |

Money in the simulator is shown with a dollar sign whatever your property's currency.

**Example: Testing 'Last minute' at The Harbour Inn**

Priya wants to see "Last minute" (**Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 3 and **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Less than** 50, **Decrease the rate** 15%) act. It measures and changes all three room types. She sets **Stay date** to tomorrow, then Standard to $150 at 40% (5 of 12), Deluxe to $200 at 30% (2 of 6) and Suite to $300 at 50% (1 of 2).

"Last minute" reads one figure for the three types together: 8 of 20 rooms, which is 40%. That is less than 50, so it fires on every room type. Standard becomes $127.50, Deluxe $170.00 and Suite $255.00.

"Busy nights" (occupancy **Greater than** 80, Increase 10%) fires on every room type. "Warm-date bump" (**Faster Than Normal** or above, Increase 10%) fires too. Standard becomes $181.50 (150, then 165, then 181.50). Deluxe becomes $242.00. Suite becomes $363.00, well under its $600 ceiling.

She switches booking speed to **Not enough history**. "Warm-date bump" moves to **Didn't fire** with "Conditions not met", and Standard becomes $165.00.

The maths is the same as a real run's, but a real night plays out over days and this is one run. The screen says so at the bottom of the results. In plain words:

- **A standard rule is shown settled.** On a real night it fires on the way into its condition and holds. Here you see where the night ends up, not each step.
A standard rule is shown settled

- **Every matching booking speed or pickup rule is added.** On a real night, when several booking speed or pickup rules match, one wins for that night and room type. Here they all fire, so the result is the most the night could move.
Every matching booking speed or pickup rule is added
- **A repeat is shown once.** A booking speed or pickup rule that is still true after its wait adjusts the night again on a real night. Here it fires once.
A repeat is shown once

- **Booking speed is a level you chose,** not a count against similar nights, so there is no "How did we know?" behind it.

The screen sums it up: "It is one run, not where a night ends up over a week." [How rules run](@39) explains what happens across a week.

**Not yet** · The simulator cannot replay a real past run, and it cannot count bookings: booking speed is a level you pick. To see what really happened on a night, read the change log entry for it and open **How did we know?**. Read [The change log](@46).
Booking speed is a level you chose,

Rules run every day of the year, for every night in the window. Every rule you build ranks the same, and the starter rules rank above yours. You cannot yet limit a rule to weekends, a date range, a season or some channels, set which rule wins, edit a rule, make an either/or rule, set an exact price, or cap how far prices move. Here is what to do instead.

**A weekend-only rule.** Every rule runs every day of the week. There is no weekday choice in the builder, and MAYA has no setting for which nights are your weekend. (In these docs, and in how similar nights are chosen, weekends are Friday and Saturday nights.) What to do instead: for a weekend price, type a price on those nights on the calendar. It becomes the base for that night, and the rules already on it are held (their changes come off). Read [Setting a price yourself](@49). For a rule that reads weekend busyness on its own, remember that booking speed already compares each Friday with other Fridays and each Saturday with other Saturdays, so a booking speed rule does not need a weekday switch to behave differently on weekends.
A weekend-only rule

**A date range, a season or an event.** Every rule runs for every night in the 60-night window, all year. What to do instead: for a wedding weekend or a festival, type a price for the range with **through…** on the calendar (up to 365 nights in one save, from tonight to 364 days ahead). Rules already on those nights are held (their changes come off), and rules that fire later stack on top, so switch off the rules that would move those nights until the weekend has passed. Switching a rule off stops it on every night, so switch it back on afterwards. Read [Hold a price for a wedding or event weekend](@67). For seasons, booking speed already compares inside the season your history shows, so a booking speed rule adjusts to the season by itself.
A date range, a season or an event

**Priority.** Every rule you build has the same priority. When two booking speed or pickup rules are true on the same night, the one with more conditions wins, then (for two pickup rules with the same **Compare**) the stricter threshold, then the bigger money move, then the older rule. The five starter rules carry a higher priority than yours, so when a starter rule and one of yours are both true on the same night and room type, the starter rule is the one that fires. Standard rules do not compete: every one whose condition holds applies. Read [How rules run](@39).
Priority

**Editing a rule.** There is no edit control. Delete the rule (which undoes its changes) and add it again. To keep its prices in place, turn it off instead and add the new one beside it. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@41).
Editing a rule

**Either/or.** Conditions on one rule are always "and": "Matches when all of the following are true." For "busy or last-minute", make two rules. Both can act on the same night, and their changes stack.
Either/or
**One night only.** A rule cannot be limited to one night. Type a price for that night instead.
One night only
**Both a percent and a fixed amount.** The form has both boxes, but when both are ticked only the percent is saved. Choose one. For "10% plus $5", make two rules. They stack.
Both a percent and a fixed amount

**An exact price, like $199.** A rule changes the price by a percent or a fixed amount, up or down. It cannot set the price to a number. For an exact price, type it on the calendar for that night, or for a run of nights with **through…**. It is published as you typed it, and rules that fire later stack on top of it. Read [Setting a price yourself](@49).
An exact price, like $199
**Copy or duplicate a rule, or copy rules to another property.** Not yet. Build the rule again. Rules belong to one property.
Copy or duplicate a rule, or copy rules to another property
**Rename a rule.** Not yet. Delete and re-add.
Rename a rule

**An occupancy threshold above 100.** The measured number can go above 100% (rooms out of service after a night sold, or overbooking), but a threshold above 100 is saved as 100. **Greater than** 100 fires on any overbooked night.
An occupancy threshold above 100

**Two conditions of the same kind.** One of each: at most one occupancy row, one booking speed row, one booking window row and one pickup row per rule. For a band such as "between 60% and 80%", the builder cannot say it. Use two rules: one at **Greater than** 60, and a second at **Greater than** 80 that makes the change you want above the band. The two stack, so choose the second amount with the first already applied.

**Example: A band with two rules**

You want Standard ($150) up $15 above 60% full, and up $30 in all above 80%. Fixed amounts add, so build two rules on Standard alone. Rule A: **Greater than** 60, **Increase the rate**, **Adjust by fixed amount ($)** 15 (untick the percent). Rule B: the same with **Greater than** 80. With 9 of 12 Standard rooms booked (75%), only rule A holds: $165. With 11 of 12 booked (92%), both hold: $180.
Two conditions of the same kind

**A cap on how far or how fast prices move.** There is no setting such as "never more than 20% below my base rate" or "at most one change a day", and a floor or ceiling cannot be a percentage. Floors and ceilings are fixed amounts, one pair per room type, the same on every night.

To keep Standard ($150) within 20% of its usual rate, it needs a $120 floor. [Email us](mailto:info@modern-hospitality-solutions.com?subject=Floor%20for%20one%20room%20type) to set it for Standard alone. Answering the floor question again would put $120 on every room type, Deluxe and Suite included. A floor is one amount for every night, so it does not follow a base rate that changes through the year. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28#where-they-are-set).

What holds prices back today:

- the floor and ceiling of each room type
A cap on how far or how fast prices move

- in each cycle, at most one booking speed or pickup rule changes a given night and room type
- once a booking speed or pickup rule has changed the same night three times, an amber banner asks you whether it should keep going

A price can still change more than once in a day. A standard rule switches on and off as bookings come and go, and a stronger rule can step in while a weaker one waits. Read [How rules run](@39) and [Floors and ceilings](@28).

**A smallest change, such as "do not send moves under 1%".** There is no minimum-change setting. Any price that changed, even by a cent, is sent to Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations once you are live. What to do instead: use larger amounts, or fewer rules that stack.
A smallest change, such as "do not send moves under 1%"

**No changes in the last few days before arrival, or at certain hours.** There is no freeze window and no quiet hours. Cycles run about every five minutes, day and night, and tonight is always priced. What you can do:

- On a booking speed or pickup rule you build, add a **Booking window (days to stay)** row set to **Greater than** 2. The rule then makes no new change on tonight or the next two nights. What it already did there stays, though a raise still comes off if enough of the bookings behind it cancel.
- On a standard rule, the same row takes the rule's change off as the night comes within those days, and that is itself a price change. A standard rule cannot be held still near arrival this way.
No changes in the last few days before arrival, or at certain hours

**Only direct bookings, or leaving out booking sites.** There is no channel filter. Every booking counts the same, whatever channel it came from: direct, through an online travel agency (a booking site), or made at the front desk. That goes for sellable occupancy, booking speed and pickup count alike.
Only direct bookings, or leaving out booking sites

**Length of stay (LOS) pricing, such as cheaper for a 7-night stay.** There is no condition for how long a guest is staying, and no minimum stay setting. MAYA writes one nightly rate per room type on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, and nothing to Mews. What to do instead: keep length-of-stay prices and minimum stays in your property system. A long-stay or discounted rate plan set up there to follow your base rate moves by your system's own rules when MAYA changes the base. Read [Prices are not reaching your property system](@99) for how a plan that follows the base rate behaves.
Length of stay (LOS) pricing, such as cheaper for a 7-night stay

**A setting for how bold MAYA is.** There is no aggressiveness setting and no slider from careful to bold. How far and how often prices move depends only on what you set: the rules, their amounts, the speed levels, the waits, and each room type's floor and ceiling. To be bolder, pick larger amounts, levels nearer Normal (such as **Faster Than Normal**), shorter waits or a higher ceiling. To be gentler, do the opposite or raise the floor. The last of the five questions asks how you want your current pricing treated, but it changes nothing today. Read [The five questions](@25) and [Your starter rules](@27).
A setting for how bold MAYA is

**A rule that raises only when a night is nearly full and booking fast.** This one you can do: put a **Sellable occupancy (%)** row and a **Booking speed (recommended)** row on the same rule. Both must be true.
A rule that raises only when a night is nearly full and booking fast

- Floors and ceilings are per room type, not per night, season or weekend. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
- Rooms out of service take rooms off the sellable count for a stretch of nights, which changes what occupancy rules see. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@51).
- Which room types count as rooms is set on the **PMS** tab.

**Good to know** · Most limits on this page are limits of the rule builder, not of the pricing. A price you type on the calendar can set an exact number, a weekend price or an event price for the nights you choose, and rules keep working around it.

Each day on the calendar shows sellable occupancy for the whole property, rooms booked over rooms you can sell, the room revenue already on the books, and a colour bar that compares the night with your own other nights. Click a day to see every room type's current price and to type a price yourself. The calendar updates on its own as bookings and prices change.
The **Calendar** tab is the first tab on the dashboard and the one MAYA opens on. Everyone on the property can see it, whatever their role.

Across the top you have **Prev** and **Next**, which step one month at a time, and two dropdowns, **Month** and **Year**. The years on offer run from the first month that has any booking or any published price to the last one. A property with no bookings or prices yet sees only the year on screen. **Prev** and **Next** still move across years.

You can open any month, past or future. What changes far ahead is not the calendar but the prices: your rules run on tonight and the next 59 nights, so nights beyond that show no current price (see "When a night has no current price" below).

On the right, once the month has loaded, a small line reads "Updated 3:05:12 PM · live". The time is your browser's clock, to the second, not the property's. Before the month loads it reads "Loading…".

The month is laid out seven days wide with Sunday in the first column. There is no row of weekday names above the grid. Count from the left with Sunday first, or click a day: the heading of the day detail names the weekday.

While the month loads, or while you switch property, a grey placeholder of the same shape stands in for the grid.

Every day is a button. From top to bottom it shows:

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| The day number | The date within the month. |
| A large percentage, such as **60%** | Sellable occupancy for the whole property: rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell that night, rounded to a whole percent. |
| "12/20 rooms" | Rooms booked, then rooms you can sell that night. |
| A dollar figure, such as "$2.2k" or "$850" | Room revenue on the books for that night. From $1,000 it is shortened to thousands with one decimal. Hover it and the label reads "Room revenue (booked nights)". |
| A thin colour bar | Green, amber or red, comparing the night with your other nights (next section). |

Two details behind those numbers matter when you check them against your property system.

**Only room types ticked as rooms are counted** in the percentage and in "12/20 rooms". A meeting room or a court that you have unticked under **Counts as a room** is left out of both. Rooms you have entered as out of service come off the sellable count for those nights. The Harbour Inn has 20 rooms across Standard, Deluxe and Suite. With 2 Standard rooms out of service and 11 rooms booked, the card reads "11/18 rooms" and 61%.
Only room types ticked as rooms are counted

**The dollar figure sums every room type**, including ones that do not count as rooms. Each booked night is valued at the rate MAYA imported with the booking, or at its current rate if none was imported.
The dollar figure sums every room type

**ThinkReservations:** The room charges ThinkReservations lists for the booking, after discounts, one night at a time. Other lines on the booking, such as separate tax, fee or extra lines, are not in it.

**Mews:** The booking's total price, taxes included, split evenly across its nights. Anything else Mews includes in that total, such as extras, is in it too.

So the figure will not match a revenue report in your system that adds taxes, fees or extras, takes off commission, or reflects a booking's rate after it was changed. A $0 comp or house-use booking adds nothing and lowers the ADR. [Occupancy looks wrong](@98) covers the occupancy side.
What that rate includes depends on your system

**A booking with no amount at all counts as $150 a night.** That happens only when your system reports a booking with no amount on it, which is not the same as $0. The $150 is a placeholder, not a rate from your system, and it is the same in every currency. It also goes into that room type's Revenue and ADR in the day detail. If a night's figure is $150 more than your system shows, look for a booking on that night with no amount.

**Good to know** · Occupancy on the day card can read over 100%. That happens when rooms were sold before a block or an out of service stretch was entered, or when your system has taken an overbooking. [Occupancy looks wrong](@98) has the detail.
A booking with no amount at all counts as $150 a night

Under the grid a legend names the three colours: "strong night" (green), "typical night" (amber) and "weak night" (red). The legend goes on to say the colour is measured by revenue per room, relative to the property's own results, and that future nights compare against other upcoming nights.

Here is how the colour is set:

- For each night, MAYA adds up the latest rate it has read for each booked room. A booked room with no rate adds nothing.
- It divides that total by the number of rooms in room types that count as rooms. That is revenue per room.
- Nights before today are compared only with other past nights. Today and later are compared only with other upcoming nights. Revenue for a future night keeps growing as bookings land, so mixing the two would paint every future night red.

- Nights inside a closed period you confirmed on the review are left out when the thirds are worked out, but they still get a colour.

The total behind the colour can differ from the dollar figure on the day card. The card uses the rate MAYA imported with each booking, and the $150 placeholder for a booking with no amount. So the two differ when a booking's rate has changed in your system since it was imported. They also differ when a booking has no amount.

The colour is not occupancy. A night can be 90% full and still red if those rooms sold cheaply against your other nights, and a half-full night with strong rates can be green.

**Good to know: Colours can lag by a few minutes** · The booked counts and dollar figures are always fresh, but a new booking can take up to 5 minutes to change a colour.

Clicking a day opens a panel under the grid. The clicked day gets a blue ring.

The heading is the full date, for example "Friday, November 13, 2026". Under it, one summary line:

"12/20 rooms · 60% sellable occupancy · revenue on the books $2,180.00"

For a night that has passed, the last part reads "revenue $2,180.00" instead of "revenue on the books". The dollar amount here is the same figure as on the day card, shown in full.

Then one card per active room type, including types that do not count as rooms. Each card shows:

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| The room type's name | With a badge beside it when a manual price is open on that night (below). |
| "Booked 8/12" | Rooms booked in this type, then rooms you can sell in this type that night. |
| "ADR $160.00" | ADR means average daily rate: this type's room revenue for the night divided by the rooms booked. When **Booked** reads 0, ignore the ADR line. It shows the $150.00 placeholder on every room type with nothing booked, whatever that type's rate. |
| "Current price $165.00" | The price your rules produce for this room type on this night, within your floor and ceiling. On Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, this is the price MAYA sends when you are live (except a price of 0, a comp night). Nothing is sent to Mews. On a night that has passed, it is the last price the night had. It shows a dash when no price has been published (next section). |
| "Revenue $1280.00" | Room revenue on the books for this type on this night. The card prints it without a thousands comma. |
| A price box, **through…**, **Save** and a **?** | The manual price editor. [Setting a price yourself](@49) explains every part of it. |

**Example: The Harbour Inn on a Friday in November**

Friday, November 13, 2026 has 12 of 20 rooms booked, so the day card reads 60% and "12/20 rooms". Standard has 8 of 12 booked at $160 a night on average, Deluxe 3 of 6 at $200, Suite 1 of 2 at $300, and the Meeting Room is unbooked. Revenue on the books is $1,280 + $600 + $300 = $2,180, so the day card reads "$2.2k" and the day detail "$2,180.00".
